title: Dependence of charge separation efficiency on the exciton-charge transfer offset and Gaussian disorder in organic solar cells
summary: State-of-the-art organic solar cells increasingly rely on low-offset semiconductor blends, challenging the traditional requirement of a large energetic driving force for efficient charge separation. In these systems, the energetic offset $ΔE_{\mathrm{LE-CT}}$ between local exciton (LE) and charge-transfer (CT) states approaches the thermal energy, making exciton-CT hybridization and thermal repopulation of the exciton level critical to device performance. In this work, we directly compare a macroscopic two-state rate model with three-dimensional kinetic Monte-Carlo (kMC) simulations to investigate microscopic charge separation dynamics and the role of Gaussian energetic disorder. We demonstrate that in the absence of disorder, the analytical rate model accurately reproduces kMC predictions for the whole range of $ΔE_{\mathrm{LE-CT}}$. Specifically, the macroscopic model successfully explains horizontal shifts in the internal quantum efficiency curves that arise depending on how the energetic offset is physically realized in the constituent molecules. We show that these variations can be captured entirely through the ratio of degeneracies of the LE and CT states, respectively. Introducing Gaussian energetic disorder into the kMC simulation reveals a distinct crossover behavior depending on $ΔE_{\mathrm{LE-CT}}$. While disorder is mostly detrimental at large offsets, it can significantly boost efficiency at intermediate and low offsets. Thermalization of charge carriers within the disorder-broadened density of states creates an effective driving force allowing charge separation even at zero or negative energetic offsets.

AI.tldr: This paper compares a macroscopic two-state rate model with 3D kinetic Monte-Carlo simulations to study charge separation in low-offset organic solar cells, finding that energetic disorder can boost efficiency at intermediate and low offsets by creating an effective driving force, even at zero or negative energetic offsets.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art organic solar cells increasingly use low-offset semiconductor blends that challenge the traditional requirement of a large energetic driving force for efficient charge separation, making it critical to understand the roles of exciton-CT hybridization and thermal repopulation in these systems.
AI.method: The authors directly compare a macroscopic two-state rate model with three-dimensional kinetic Monte-Carlo simulations to investigate charge separation dynamics and the role of Gaussian energetic disorder across varying ΔE_{LE-CT} values.
AI.result: (1) Without disorder, the analytical rate model accurately reproduces kMC predictions across all ΔE_{LE-CT}. (2) Horizontal shifts in IQE curves are explained by the ratio of degeneracies of LE and CT states. (3) Disorder is detrimental at large offsets but significantly boosts efficiency at intermediate and low offsets. (4) Thermalization within the disorder-broadened density of states creates an effective driving force enabling charge separation even at zero or negative offsets.
AI.conclusion: Gaussian energetic disorder can be beneficial for low-offset organic solar cells by creating an effective driving force through carrier thermalization, enabling efficient charge separation even when the intrinsic energetic offset is zero or negative.

title: Non-self-averaging topological Anderson insulator
summary: Current research on the disordered topological quantum phases primarily focuses on the uncorrelated and short-range correlated disorder regime. These topological Anderson insulators are typically self-averaging. However, topological quantum systems with long-range correlated disorder have received limited attention due to the absence of tractable analytical methods. In fact, the long-range correlated disorder introduces more complex effects on topological quantum states. Here, we demonstrate that the long-range correlated disorder could induce anomalously statistical feature where the topological Anderson states become non-self-averaging, and the phase diagram is strongly dependent on individual disorder configurations. We term this statistical phase the non-self-averaging topological Anderson insulator. The non-self-averaging property is identified by the non-vanishing finite values of the relative variance of the Lyapunov exponent in the thermodynamic limit, alongside the non-Gaussian distributions of the Lyapunov exponent. Consequently, the topological properties of a single disordered sample deviate from the ensemble average, causing a breakdown of the central limit theorem. The non-self-averaging topological Anderson insulator provides insights into the interplay between correlated disorder and topology.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a new statistical phase called the non-self-averaging topological Anderson insulator, induced by long-range correlated disorder, where topological Anderson states exhibit non-self-averaging behavior, non-Gaussian Lyapunov exponent distributions, and a breakdown of the central limit theorem.
AI.motivation: While topological Anderson insulators in uncorrelated and short-range correlated disorder regimes are well-studied and self-averaging, long-range correlated disorder introduces more complex effects that have received limited attention due to the lack of tractable analytical methods.
AI.method: The authors analyze the statistical properties of the Lyapunov exponent in the thermodynamic limit, specifically examining the relative variance and distribution shapes to identify non-self-averaging behavior.
AI.result: Long-range correlated disorder induces non-self-averaging topological Anderson states, characterized by non-vanishing relative variance of the Lyapunov exponent and non-Gaussian distributions in the thermodynamic limit, causing the phase diagram to become strongly dependent on individual disorder configurations.
AI.conclusion: The discovery of the non-self-averaging topological Anderson insulator reveals a breakdown of the central limit theorem in topological quantum systems with long-range correlated disorder, providing new insights into the interplay between correlated disorder and topological phases.

title: Quantum-Informed Portfolio Selection: An End-to-End Pipeline Validated on Trapped-Ion Hardware with Real Market Data
summary: Portfolio diversification - a cornerstone of modern investment management - can be formulated as a Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem on asset correlation graphs. Solving this problem at scale is computationally challenging, motivating the exploration of quantum algorithms for practical financial optimization. We propose an end-to-end pipeline leveraging qReduMIS, a recursive hybrid quantum-classical algorithm. Rather than using quantum optimization to directly produce a final solution, qReduMIS leverages independent set measurements from the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) to identify frozen nodes - vertices likely to belong to optimal solutions - thereby guiding and unblocking subsequent (provably optimal) classical reductions on the remaining graph. We benchmark qReduMIS on real financial data from four major market indices with up to 225 assets, executing experiments on Quantinuum's 98-qubit trapped-ion Helios system, with QAOA circuits acting on kernels of up to 78 qubits and 1016 two-qubit gates. While standalone QAOA fails to find the optimal solution for two of the largest indices (S&P 100 and Nikkei 225), qReduMIS achieves success probabilities of $0.40$ and $0.95$, respectively, with average approximation ratios $\geq 0.96$ across all four indices. We perform a systematic benchmark on the Quantinuum H2-1 noisy emulator over 73 asset correlation graphs of varying size showing that, for $p=2$ QAOA layers, the optimal time-to-solution scaling exponent of qReduMIS is $3.2$ times smaller than that of standalone QAOA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes qReduMIS, a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm that uses QAOA to identify frozen nodes in asset correlation graphs, enabling optimal classical reductions for portfolio diversification via Maximum Independent Set. Tested on real financial data from four major indices on Quantinuum's 98-qubit Helios system, qReduMIS achieves success probabilities up to 0.95 and approximation ratios ≥0.96 where standalone QAOA fails, with a 3.2× better time-to-solution scaling exponent.
AI.motivation: Portfolio diversification, formulated as a Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem on asset correlation graphs, is computationally challenging at scale. This motivates exploring quantum algorithms for practical financial optimization.
AI.method: qReduMIS recursively applies QAOA to measure independent sets, identifies frozen nodes (vertices likely in optimal solutions), and uses these to guide and unblock provably optimal classical reductions on the remaining graph.
AI.result: On real financial data from four indices (up to 225 assets), executed on Quantinuum's 98-qubit Helios system with QAOA circuits up to 78 qubits and 1016 two-qubit gates, qReduMIS achieves success probabilities of 0.40 (S&P 100) and 0.95 (Nikkei 225) where standalone QAOA fails, with average approximation ratios ≥0.96. On 73 graphs with p=2 QAOA layers, qReduMIS has a 3.2× smaller optimal time-to-solution scaling exponent than standalone QAOA.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid quantum-classical qReduMIS algorithm significantly outperforms standalone QAOA for large-scale portfolio diversification (MIS) problems, offering better scalability and success probability through quantum-guided classical reduction.

title: Quantum Amplitude Estimation in Gradient-Based Stochastic Optimization
summary: In this paper we prove, both mathematically and through a simulation, how the Quantum Amplitude Estimation algorithm can obtain quadratic improvements with respect to the Monte Carlo method in gradient-based stochastic optimization, highlighting the central role of the Quantum Phase Estimation concentration guarantee in achieving the predicted advantage.

AI.tldr: This paper proves mathematically and via simulation that the Quantum Amplitude Estimation algorithm achieves quadratic improvement over Monte Carlo in gradient-based stochastic optimization, with Quantum Phase Estimation concentration being key to this advantage.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate and prove that Quantum Amplitude Estimation can provide quadratic speedups over classical Monte Carlo methods in the context of gradient-based stochastic optimization.
AI.method: Mathematical proof and simulation comparing Quantum Amplitude Estimation against Monte Carlo methods for gradient-based stochastic optimization, with analysis of Quantum Phase Estimation concentration guarantees.
AI.result: Quantum Amplitude Estimation achieves quadratic improvements in convergence rate compared to Monte Carlo methods for gradient-based stochastic optimization.
AI.conclusion: The Quantum Phase Estimation concentration guarantee is central to realizing the predicted quadratic advantage, confirming the practical viability of quantum speedup for stochastic optimization tasks.

title: Quantum Reconstruction and Phenomenology per the Relativity Principle
summary: We use the relativity principle to complete axiomatic reconstructions of quantum mechanics (QM) via information-theoretic principles that are based on Darrigol's "discreteness" requirement or its equivalent, e.g., Brukner & Zeilinger's Information Invariance & Continuity or Khrennikov's quantum action invariance principle. In this approach to the quantum reconstruction program (QRP), the Hilbert space kinematics of QM is derived most fundamentally from the experimentally motivated postulate of "discreteness," rendering QM a principle theory as defined by Einstein. Special relativity is also a principle theory, since its Lorentz transformation kinematics is derived from the experimentally motivated light postulate. While special relativity has a compelling fundamental principle (relativity principle) to account for its experimentally motivated light postulate, QRP has not produced a compelling fundamental principle to account for its experimentally motivated "discreteness" requirement. We complete QRP by showing how the "discreteness" requirement is necessitated by the relativity principle and Planck's radiation law, just like the light postulate is necessitated by the relativity principle and Maxwell's equations. Accordingly, the fundamental explanans for time dilation, length contraction, quantum superposition, and entanglement is the relativity principle. Phenomenologically speaking, the relativity principle is "the equality of all perspectives." Thus, quantum entanglement isn't evidence for the violation of intersubjective agreement or the need to abandon factive or objective models of reality, as in relational interpretations of QM. It is evidence that reality is not a fragmented collage of different subjective experiences from different perspectives, it's a comprehensive and coherent integration of those different subjective experiences per the equality of all perspectives.

AI.tldr: The paper completes axiomatic reconstructions of QM by showing that the "discreteness" requirement (foundational to deriving Hilbert space kinematics) is necessitated by the relativity principle and Planck's radiation law, analogous to how the light postulate arises from relativity and Maxwell's equations. This makes the relativity principle the fundamental explanans for quantum phenomena like superposition and entanglement, implying that reality is a coherent integration of all perspectives rather than fragmented subjective experiences.
AI.motivation: While quantum reconstruction programs (QRP) have derived QM from the experimentally motivated "discreteness" postulate (making QM a principle theory), they lack a compelling fundamental principle to account for this discreteness requirement — unlike special relativity, which has the relativity principle to justify its light postulate. The paper aims to fill this gap.
AI.method: The authors show that the discreteness requirement in QRP is necessitated by combining the relativity principle with Planck's radiation law, structurally analogous to how the light postulate is necessitated by the relativity principle and Maxwell's equations. They compare the logical structure of special relativity and quantum reconstruction programs to demonstrate this parallel.
AI.result: The relativity principle (equality of all perspectives) is identified as the fundamental principle accounting for discreteness, making it the foundational explanans for quantum superposition and entanglement. This refutes relational interpretations that view entanglement as violating objectivity — instead, entanglement demonstrates the comprehensive integration of different perspectives into a coherent reality.
AI.conclusion: Quantum entanglement does not indicate a need to abandon objective models of reality or intersubjective agreement; rather, it shows that reality coherently integrates all perspectives per the equality of all perspectives. The relativity principle unifies the foundations of both special relativity and quantum mechanics as principle theories.

title: Comment on "Ideal clocks -- a convenient fiction" by K. Lorek et al
comment: 5 pages, published version. Comment on arXiv:1503.01025
summary: We correct a subtle oversight in Eq.(19) of K. Lorek et al. [Class. Quantum Grav. 32 175003 (2015)] concerning the decay probability of a uniformly accelerated quantum clock. The original expression included unphysical cross-wedge term ($|\barγ_{K 1}|^2$) violating the spatial separation of Rindler wedges. We derive the corrected probability using the paper's Rindler conformal coordinates $(τ, ξ)$, retaining only causally consistent thermal terms, and discuss implications for relativistic clock models.

AI.tldr: This paper corrects an error in Eq.(19) of Lorek et al. (2015) regarding the decay probability of a uniformly accelerated quantum clock, where an unphysical cross-wedge term violated Rindler wedge causality. The corrected probability retains only causally consistent thermal terms using Rindler conformal coordinates, with implications for relativistic clock models.
AI.motivation: To correct a subtle but important oversight in the original expression for the decay probability of a uniformly accelerated quantum clock, specifically the inclusion of an unphysical cross-wedge term that violates the causal structure of Rindler wedges.
AI.method: The authors derive the corrected decay probability using Rindler conformal coordinates (τ, ξ) from the original paper, systematically removing the cross-wedge term |γ̄_{K1}|² that incorrectly coupled spacelike-separated Rindler wedges, retaining only causally consistent thermal contributions.
AI.result: A corrected decay probability formula for a uniformly accelerated quantum clock that respects the causal separation of Rindler wedges, eliminating the unphysical cross-wedge term present in the original Eq.(19).
AI.conclusion: The corrected expression has implications for relativistic clock models, ensuring that accelerated clock decay calculations remain causally consistent with the Unruh effect and the structure of Rindler spacetime.

title: Spectral Geometry and Bosonic-Bloch Probes: Explorations in Quantum Learning
summary: This paper studies how spectral geometry emerges in quantum learning models and how it can be diagnosed with physically grounded probes. In graph-regularized quantum networks, training reorganizes the output similarity graph, increases the effective spectral dimension Delta S = +0.23, and reshapes the Laplacian spectrum. Edge-resolved two-boson interference directly probes this restructuring: the bosonic enhancement Delta P_uv correlates with the Fiedler edge split |Delta v_2| (r = -0.50), linking learned spectral partitions to interference signatures. A phase diagram shows a nonmonotonic dependence of performance on coupling strength gamma and noise delta, with graph regularization improving fidelity only in a restricted regime; hardware experiments confirm the predicted interference behavior within shot-noise uncertainty. We also analyze a hybrid quantum autoencoder and introduce Bloch-space drift as a geometric diagnostic of its latent representation. With an unsupervised benign-data threshold, the model achieves high ranking performance (ROC-AUC about 0.99) and negligible false-negative rates. Absolute Bloch drift strongly discriminates anomalies (ROC-AUC at least about 0.9), while consecutive drift is near random (ROC-AUC about 0.5), showing that detection arises from persistent state-space displacement rather than local fluctuations. Through the geometry of reduced single-qubit states and associated quantum Fisher information, these results show that learning-induced spectral organization appears as measurable quantum-state structure, establishing a unified spectral-geometric framework for diagnosing quantum learning systems with bosonic and Bloch probes.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that quantum learning models reorganize spectral geometry, measurable via bosonic interference and Bloch drift probes. Training increases effective spectral dimension (+0.23) and reshapes Laplacian spectra. Two-boson interference correlates with spectral partitions (r=-0.50). A hybrid quantum autoencoder uses Bloch drift as a geometric diagnostic, achieving ROC-AUC ~0.99 for anomaly detection with persistent state-space displacement as the key discriminator.
AI.motivation: To understand how spectral geometry emerges in quantum learning models and to develop physically grounded probes (bosonic interference and Bloch drift) for diagnosing such geometric restructuring during training.
AI.method: Graph-regularized quantum networks with spectral analysis of output similarity; edge-resolved two-boson interference to probe spectral partitions; hybrid quantum autoencoder with Bloch-space drift as geometric diagnostic; unsupervised benign-data thresholding; hardware experiments for interference validation.
AI.result: Effective spectral dimension increases by +0.23 after training; bosonic enhancement correlates with Fiedler edge split (r=-0.50); graph regularization improves fidelity only in a restricted (γ, δ) regime; hybrid autoencoder achieves ROC-AUC ~0.99 with negligible false negatives; absolute Bloch drift gives ROC-AUC ≥~0.9 while consecutive drift gives ~0.5.
AI.conclusion: Learning-induced spectral reorganization manifests as measurable quantum-state structure, unifying bosonic and Bloch probes into a spectral-geometric framework for diagnosing quantum learning systems.

title: Velocity of a Quantum Particle in a Classically Forbidden Region
summary: Recently, Sharoglazova et al. [Nature 643, 67 (2025)] proposed a procedure for determining the speed of a quantum particle in the classically forbidden region of a potential step, and implemented it in a beautiful experiment. The inferred speeds disagree significantly with the Bohmian velocities, which the authors presented as an experimental challenge to Bohmian mechanics. This is puzzling because the speeds are inferred from particle populations in coupled waveguides for which Bohmian mechanics and standard quantum mechanics make identical predictions. We resolve the puzzle by a detailed theoretical analysis of the experimental setup. We show that the speed inference rests on an assumption that fails in the relevant (evanescent) regime according to both Bohmian mechanics and standard quantum mechanics -- namely that the inter-waveguide tunneling time is set by the transverse coupling and is not affected by entanglement with the longitudinal degree of freedom. We also consider a second speed estimate suggested by Sharoglazova et al., which is based on the Büttiker dwell time formula for particles in the forbidden region. We show that the authors applied the formula incorrectly, and that a correct application yields exact agreement with the predictions of Bohmian mechanics. Our analysis includes explicit calculations of Bohmian trajectories, dwell times, and longitudinal speeds in the two-dimensional waveguide model of the experiment.

AI.tldr: The authors resolve a puzzle from Sharoglazova et al. (Nature 2025) which claimed experimental speeds of quantum particles in a forbidden region challenge Bohmian mechanics. They show the speed inference relies on a false assumption about tunneling time, and a correct application of the Büttiker dwell time formula yields agreement with Bohmian predictions.
AI.motivation: To resolve the apparent discrepancy between experimental speed measurements reported by Sharoglazova et al. and the predictions of Bohmian mechanics for a quantum particle in the classically forbidden region of a potential step.
AI.method: Detailed theoretical analysis of the experimental waveguide setup, examining assumptions underlying speed inference (specifically inter-waveguide tunneling time independence from longitudinal entanglement), and correcting the application of the Büttiker dwell time formula, supported by explicit 2D Bohmian trajectory and dwell time calculations.
AI.result: (1) The speed inference method used by Sharoglazova et al. relies on an assumption that inter-waveguide tunneling time is set solely by transverse coupling, which fails in the evanescent regime in both Bohmian and standard quantum mechanics. (2) The Büttiker dwell time formula was applied incorrectly; correct application yields exact agreement with Bohmian mechanics.
AI.conclusion: The experimental results do not pose a valid challenge to Bohmian mechanics; the apparent disagreement arises from flawed assumptions and incorrect application of standard formulas, not from a failure of the Bohmian framework.

title: Optically Active Single Hole Spin in ZnSe
summary: Semiconductor hole spins offer a pathway to extended coherence times by decoupling from nuclear magnetic noise, while their spin-orbit coupling enables fast all-electrical control. In ZnSe, however, realizing this potential has been limited by p-doping challenges. Here, we circumvent this limit by optically activating acceptors within the ZnSe quantum well. We isolate a single-hole spin bound to a shallow acceptor, confirmed by antibunching and accessed via the fast (244 ps) radiative recombination of a bound exciton. Magnetic and Raman spectroscopy of the ground state reveal an effective hole g-factor of 0.7 and an optical resonance linewidth of 26.7 GHz. Complementary first-principles simulations, together with the experimental results, provide evidence that points toward nitrogen as the most likely acceptor impurity. These results introduce a promising new platform for optically active spin qubits and single-photon sources in ZnSe.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates optically active single-hole spins bound to shallow acceptors in ZnSe quantum wells, achieving fast radiative recombination (244 ps), a hole g-factor of 0.7, and 26.7 GHz optical linewidth, with first-principles simulations identifying nitrogen as the likely acceptor impurity.
AI.motivation: Semiconductor hole spins can achieve extended coherence times by decoupling from nuclear magnetic noise and enable fast all-electrical control via spin-orbit coupling, but realizing this potential in ZnSe has been limited by p-doping challenges.
AI.method: Optically activated acceptors within ZnSe quantum wells; isolated single-hole spin bound to a shallow acceptor confirmed by antibunching; accessed via bound exciton radiative recombination (244 ps); characterized using magnetic and Raman spectroscopy; complemented by first-principles simulations.
AI.result: Effective hole g-factor of 0.7; optical resonance linewidth of 26.7 GHz; nitrogen identified as the most likely acceptor impurity via combined experimental and simulation evidence.
AI.conclusion: This work introduces a promising new platform for optically active spin qubits and single-photon sources in ZnSe.

title: Work Statistics Under Quantum-Jump and Quench Dynamics in Monitored Ising Chains
summary: We investigate work statistics in monitored transverse-field Ising chains subject to both a quantum quench of the transverse field and either stochastic quantum jumps or controlled measurement sequences. For generalized measurements, we derive a trajectory-resolved generating function for work statistics in the two-point energy measurement scheme. Evaluating it using a fermionic Gaussian-state formalism, we show that, under stochastic jump dynamics, the work distribution crosses over from a comb-like structure to an essentially Gaussian form with shrinking sub-Gaussian tails, as the number of detection events grows. For controlled jump protocols, the energy added by each jump is constant when successive jumps are causally disconnected but decreases and then saturates when they lie within each other's light cone, yielding linear and sublinear growth of the average work, respectively. For monitored quenches, continuous observation washes out the fine structure of the isolated-quench distribution and again drives the statistics toward Gaussian behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper studies work statistics in monitored transverse-field Ising chains under quantum quenches and measurement sequences, showing that stochastic jumps drive work distributions from comb-like to Gaussian forms, while controlled jumps yield linear or sublinear work growth depending on causal connectivity within light cones.
AI.motivation: To understand how measurement and monitoring affect work statistics in quantum many-body systems, specifically how stochastic and controlled jump dynamics modify the energy exchange distribution during quantum quenches.
AI.method: Derives a trajectory-resolved generating function for work statistics using a two-point energy measurement scheme, evaluated via a fermionic Gaussian-state formalism for generalized measurements in transverse-field Ising chains.
AI.result: Under stochastic jumps, the work distribution transitions from a comb-like structure to a Gaussian form with shrinking sub-Gaussian tails as detection events increase. For controlled jumps, energy added per jump is constant when jumps are causally disconnected, but decreases and saturates within each other's light cone, yielding linear and sublinear work growth. Continuous observation washes out fine structure and drives Gaussian behavior.
AI.conclusion: Monitoring and measurement protocols fundamentally reshape work statistics in quantum quenches, with the crossover to Gaussian behavior being a universal feature, and causal structure dictating energy accumulation patterns in controlled settings.

title: Superconducting Spiral Inductors for RF Reflectometry: Operation at Elevated Temperatures and Magnetic Fields
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, includes main manuscript and appendices
summary: Superconducting spiral inductors are emerging as key components for radio-frequency (RF) reflectometry, a widely used readout technique for semiconductor spin qubits. Future scalable quantum-computing architectures are expected to operate at elevated temperatures and magnetic fields, placing new demands on the performance and stability of superconducting circuit elements. Here, we present a systematic study of NbTiN spiral inductors under temperatures of several kelvin and magnetic fields approaching 1 T. By combining weakly coupled resonator measurements with independent two-port inductance extraction, we separate inductive and capacitive contributions to device behaviour and directly identify the origin of resonance shifts and quality factor degradation. Furthermore, we establish practical design metrics linking geometry, temperature sensitivity, and magnetic-field robustness. These results provide a general framework for benchmarking superconducting inductors and guiding the design of future RF-reflectometry circuits for practical quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies NbTiN spiral inductors under elevated temperatures (several kelvin) and high magnetic fields (up to ~1 T), separating inductive and capacitive effects to identify origins of resonance shifts and Q-factor degradation, and provides design metrics for RF-reflectometry readout in scalable quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Future scalable quantum-computing architectures using RF reflectometry for spin-qubit readout require superconducting spiral inductors that operate reliably at elevated temperatures and high magnetic fields, yet the performance and stability of these inductors under such conditions are not well understood.
AI.method: The study combines weakly coupled resonator measurements with independent two-port inductance extraction to separate inductive and capacitive contributions to device behavior, enabling identification of the origins of resonance shifts and quality factor degradation in NbTiN spiral inductors.
AI.result: The authors establish practical design metrics linking geometry, temperature sensitivity, and magnetic-field robustness, providing a quantitative understanding of how these factors affect inductor performance.
AI.conclusion: These results offer a general framework for benchmarking superconducting inductors and guiding the design of future RF-reflectometry circuits for practical quantum technologies operating under demanding thermal and magnetic conditions.

title: A universal time-of-arrival signature of Bose--Einstein condensation
summary: We show that Bose--Einstein condensation produces a cusp in the time-of-arrival (TOA) statistics of a harmonically trapped gas released into free fall. In the semiclassical long time-of-flight regime, with $ε=σ_V/\sqrt{2gH}\ll1$, both the mean and standard deviation of the arrival time distribution, which are governed by the longitudinal velocity variance, remain continuous, but acquire a cusp whose one-sided slope ratio is universal within the ideal-gas far-field limit, $\mathcal{R}_\infty=2.5556\ldots$, and equals the trapped-gas specific-heat ratio $C(Tc^-)/C(Tc^+)$. Finite atom number rounds the cusp and weak interactions perturb it only weakly, leaving a measurable time-domain signature of condensation.

AI.tldr: Bose-Einstein condensation creates a cusp in time-of-arrival statistics of a falling gas, with a universal slope ratio equal to the specific-heat ratio.
AI.motivation: To identify a measurable time-domain signature of Bose-Einstein condensation in free-fall expansion experiments.
AI.method: Analytical and semiclassical analysis of time-of-arrival statistics in the far-field limit (ε ≪ 1), examining mean and standard deviation of arrival time distribution for a harmonically trapped gas released into free fall.
AI.result: Both mean and standard deviation of TOA remain continuous at Tc but develop a cusp. The one-sided slope ratio at the cusp is universal in the ideal-gas far-field limit (ℛ∞ = 2.5556...), equaling the trapped-gas specific-heat ratio C(Tc⁻)/C(Tc⁺). Finite atom number rounds the cusp; weak interactions perturb it only weakly.
AI.conclusion: The cusp in TOA statistics provides a measurable, robust time-domain signature of Bose-Einstein condensation.

title: TCL4 Asymptotic Redundancy and Canonically Consistent Master Equations
summary:
Left alone, open quantum systems relax toward a Kubo--Martin--Schwinger (KMS) equilibrium state, yet the inner workings of this process remain opaque. It remains unclear why the intricate fourth-order time-convolutionless (TCL4) population generator reproduces the comparatively simple second-order stationary state corrections. Even more surprisingly, stationary-state corrections of such precision can be compressed into a simple virtual coherence pathway: an open quantum systems analogue of virtual transitions, in which populations communicate through coherences that are never occupied.
  Here we show that this simplification arises through a sequence of stationary-state-preserving transformations that progressively eliminate asymptotically redundant components while preserving the stationary state, ultimately yielding the virtual coherence pathway. This resolves the longstanding stationary-state problem of the Redfield equation and reveals that much of the apparent complexity of the TCL4 generator is asymptotically redundant.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the stationary-state problem of the Redfield equation by showing that the complexity of the TCL4 population generator is asymptotically redundant. Through stationary-state-preserving transformations, the dynamics simplify to a virtual coherence pathway, where populations communicate via coherences that are never occupied.
AI.motivation: To understand why the intricate TCL4 population generator produces simple second-order stationary-state corrections, and to resolve the longstanding stationary-state problem of the Redfield equation.
AI.method: The authors apply a sequence of stationary-state-preserving transformations to progressively eliminate asymptotically redundant components while preserving the stationary state, ultimately yielding the virtual coherence pathway.
AI.result: The complexity of the TCL4 generator is largely asymptotically redundant; the stationary-state corrections can be compressed into a simple virtual coherence pathway analogous to virtual transitions in open quantum systems.
AI.conclusion: The longstanding stationary-state problem of the Redfield equation is resolved, and much of the apparent complexity in higher-order generators is revealed to be asymptotically unnecessary.

title: Wavefunctions localization, and the Wigner's Friend Paradox in a Framework of Discrete-Space Hypothesis
summary: We present a resolution of the Wigner's Friend paradox within a framework of quantum mechanics (QM) on the hybrid space RxQ_{p}, where Q_{p} denotes the field of p-adic numbers, regarded as a model of discrete microscopic space at the Planck-Bronstein scale. In this framework, wavefunction collapse is not an independent postulate but a dynamical consequence of the Schrödinger equation with non-local Hamiltonians: wavefunctions localize onto compact supports during measurement interactions, producing definite pointer readings without the intervention of observers or the exchange of information between subsystems. We model both Wigner and his Friend as classical apparatuses and show that each produces a definite reading through independent applications of the collapse mechanism, thereby eliminating the conflict between their descriptions of reality. The framework is consistent with the principal no-go theorems in finite- and infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces associated with extended Wigner's Friend scenarios -- including those of Frauchiger-Renner, Brukner, Bong et al., and Guérin et al. -- since it requires no agents capable of recording or reasoning about outcomes, thereby vacating the observer-dependent assumptions that drive those theorems. We illustrate the collapse mechanism explicitly through a toy model of a particle in a box, comparing the standard description with the new one. The non-locality intrinsic to QM on L2(RxQ_{p}) permits realism at the cost of locality, and the Absoluteness of Observed Events holds in our framework without requiring observer independence.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves Wigner's Friend paradox using quantum mechanics on the hybrid space R×Qₚ (real × p-adic numbers), where wavefunction collapse emerges dynamically from non-local Hamiltonians, eliminating the need for observer-dependent assumptions and circumventing major no-go theorems.
AI.motivation: To resolve the Wigner's Friend paradox and related extended Wigner's Friend scenarios (Frauchiger-Renner, Brukner, Bong et al., Guérin et al.) without invoking observer-dependent assumptions, by constructing a framework where collapse is a dynamical process rather than an independent postulate.
AI.method: The authors propose QM on L²(R×Qₚ) (real numbers × p-adic numbers), treating the p-adic component as a model of Planck-Bronstein scale discrete spacetime. Wavefunction collapse occurs dynamically via the Schrödinger equation with non-local Hamiltonians, localizing wavefunctions onto compact supports during measurement interactions. Both Wigner and his Friend are modeled as classical apparatuses, each producing definite readings independently.
AI.result: The framework yields definite pointer readings without observers or information exchange; it avoids conflict between Wigner's and the Friend's descriptions of reality. It vacates the assumptions (agents capable of recording/reasoning about outcomes) that drive the Frauchiger-Renner, Brukner, Bong et al., and Guérin et al. no-go theorems. A toy model of a particle in a box illustrates the collapse mechanism explicitly.
AI.conclusion: Non-locality intrinsic to QM on L²(R×Qₚ) permits realism at the cost of locality, and the Absoluteness of Observed Events holds without requiring observer independence. The framework is consistent with all major no-go theorems for extended Wigner's Friend scenarios.

title: Classification and Exact Local Masking in Finite-Field Clifford Dual-Unitary Circuits
summary:
We classify two-qudit finite-field Clifford dual-unitary gates and apply the classification to exact local masking and operator transport in homogeneous brickwork circuits. Under ordered one-qudit Clifford equivalence, the dual-unitary locus contains $q-2$ perfect-tensor cores, one rank-one core, and one SWAP core. The perfect cores are indexed by \[ δ=\det B=\det C, \] and are related to the ordered cross-ratio $λ$ of the associated $[4,2,3]_q$ MDS configuration through \[ λ=\fracδ{δ-1}. \] Homogeneous repetition separates these cores into five transport phases whose algebraic codimensions in $\operatorname{Sp}(4,q)$ are $0,1,2,3,4$.
  The one-site Weyl edge channels determine exact local-masking distances. Perfect-tensor circuits attain \[ d_1(t)=4t, \qquad d_2(t)=4t-2, \] whereas delayed erasers satisfy \[ d_1(t)=4t-2, \qquad d_2(t)=4t-4 \] for $t\geq 2$. Consequently, sufficiently short quantum messages are completely hidden from every one- or two-qudit output subsystem, even when the input is entangled with a reference, while remaining exactly recoverable from the full output.
  For $q=3$, we construct an explicit perfect-tensor Clifford gate from two inverse SUM gates. Exhaustive Weyl-support searches for $t=1,2,3$ reproduce the predicted masking distances, and a one-period Choi-channel calculation for a four-qutrit periodic circuit gives numerical residual leakage below $2\times 10^{-16}$. Under the coherent perturbation considered here, local leakage is linear in the perturbation strength, whereas the infidelity of recovery using the ideal inverse is quadratic near the perfect point.

AI.tldr: Two-qudit Clifford dual-unitary gates are classified, revealing q-2 perfect-tensor cores, one rank-one core, and one SWAP core. Perfect-tensor circuits achieve exact local masking with distances d₁(t)=4t, d₂(t)=4t-2, hiding quantum messages from one- or two-qudit subsystems while allowing full recovery. An explicit q=3 perfect-tensor gate is constructed and verified numerically.
AI.motivation: To classify two-qudit Clifford dual-unitary gates and apply the classification to exact local masking and operator transport in homogeneous brickwork circuits.
AI.method: Classification under ordered one-qudit Clifford equivalence; analysis of dual-unitary locus containing perfect-tensor cores, rank-one core, and SWAP core; Weyl edge channel analysis for masking distances; explicit gate construction using inverse SUM gates for q=3; exhaustive Weyl-support searches; Choi-channel calculation for residual leakage.
AI.result: The dual-unitary locus contains q-2 perfect-tensor cores (indexed by δ=det B=det C, related to cross-ratio λ=δ/(δ-1)), one rank-one core, and one SWAP core. Homogeneous repetition yields five transport phases with algebraic codimensions 0-4 in Sp(4,q). Perfect-tensor circuits achieve d₁(t)=4t, d₂(t)=4t-2; delayed erasers yield d₁(t)=4t-2, d₂(t)=4t-4. For q=3, a perfect-tensor Clifford gate is constructed; numerical tests confirm predicted masking distances and show residual leakage <2×10⁻¹⁶. Local leakage scales linearly with perturbation strength; recovery infidelity scales quadratically.
AI.conclusion: The classification exhaustively characterizes two-qudit Clifford dual-unitary gates and demonstrates that perfect-tensor circuits enable exact local masking—hiding quantum messages from one- or two-qudit subsystems while maintaining exact recoverability from the full output. The explicit q=3 construction and numerical verification confirm the theoretical predictions.

title: Learning Low-Energy Subspace Overlaps in Many-Body Systems with Measurement-Based and Coherent Quantum Strategies
summary: Predicting the overlap of quantum states with specified low-energy subspaces is a key diagnostic for quantum many-body dynamics, with direct applications in state preparation, subspace-based algorithms, and the study of thermalization. We study the supervised prediction of subspace overlaps O_K between time-evolved states and K-dimensional low-energy eigenspaces of a 10-qubit Heisenberg spin chain following a local perturbation. We compare two quantum information extraction strategies: measurement-based learning, in which classical shadow features are processed by convolutional neural networks, and coherent quantum learning, in which quantum convolutional neural networks process the state directly. We further introduce physics-informed variants for both approaches, including Hamiltonian-aware shadows and QCNN gates aligned with the Heisenberg exchange structure. Across five dataset configurations spanning weak, moderate, and strong quench regimes, physics-informed QCNNs achieve stable performance, with mean test-set coefficients of determination R^2 = 0.753-0.846. Shadow-based methods show stronger regime dependence: they outperform QCNNs in the moderate-quench regime, reaching R^2 = 0.886, but underperform in weak and strong quenches at default shot budgets, where the best shadow results are R^2 = 0.615 and 0.672, respectively. Hardware validation on Quantinuum and IBM noise models shows that arbitrary state preparation is the dominant limitation, requiring approximately 2,044 two-qubit gates and causing near-complete depolarization before inference. These results identify a regime-dependent tradeoff between measurement-based and coherent quantum learning, with shadow methods excelling when the target remains locally accessible and physics-informed QCNNs providing more robust performance across dynamical regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper studies supervised prediction of subspace overlaps between time-evolved states and low-energy eigenspaces in a 10-qubit Heisenberg spin chain, comparing measurement-based learning (classical shadows + CNNs) with coherent quantum learning (quantum convolutional neural networks). Physics-informed variants are introduced. Results show a regime-dependent tradeoff: shadow methods excel in moderate quenches (R²=0.886), while physics-informed QCNNs provide stable performance across weak, moderate, and strong quench regimes (R²=0.753-0.846). Hardware validation reveals arbitrary state preparation as the dominant bottleneck due to ~2,044 two-qubit gates causing near-complete depolarization.
AI.motivation: Predicting overlap of quantum states with low-energy subspaces is a key diagnostic for quantum many-body dynamics, with applications in state preparation, subspace-based algorithms, and studying thermalization.
AI.method: Compared two quantum information extraction strategies: (1) measurement-based learning using classical shadow features processed by CNNs, and (2) coherent quantum learning using QCNNs processing states directly. Introduced physics-informed variants including Hamiltonian-aware shadows and QCNN gates aligned with Heisenberg exchange structure. Tested on 10-qubit Heisenberg spin chain across weak, moderate, and strong quench regimes.
AI.result: Physics-informed QCNNs achieved stable performance with mean test-set R²=0.753-0.846 across all regimes. Shadow-based methods showed stronger regime dependence: outperformed QCNNs in moderate quench (R²=0.886) but underperformed in weak (R²=0.615) and strong (R²=0.672) quenches at default shot budgets. Hardware validation showed ~2,044 two-qubit gates caused near-complete depolarization before inference.
AI.conclusion: A regime-dependent tradeoff exists between measurement-based and coherent quantum learning: shadow methods excel when target is locally accessible, while physics-informed QCNNs provide more robust performance across dynamical regimes. Arbitrary state preparation is the dominant bottleneck for hardware implementation.

title: Quantum-advantage resource of a two-mode Gaussian state: Analytical theory of convex optimization and a Galois no-go for the closed-form solution
summary: We study the problem of extracting a quantum complexity resource from a mixed Gaussian state of the multimode light. We present the first complete, certificate-checked solution to this problem in a genuinely coupled sector. We carry this out for the two-mode case, the smallest case in which modes are genuinely coupled. Even in this case the solution is highly nontrivial, and we rigorously prove that it cannot be given in a closed form.

AI.tldr: The paper studies extracting quantum complexity from mixed Gaussian states in multimode light, presenting the first complete, certificate-checked solution for the two-mode case (smallest genuinely coupled case), and rigorously proves it cannot be expressed in closed form.
AI.motivation: To address the difficulty of extracting quantum complexity resources from mixed Gaussian states, particularly in genuinely coupled modes where prior solutions were incomplete or lacked certificate checking.
AI.method: The authors develop a certificate-checked approach to extract quantum complexity from mixed Gaussian states, demonstrated on the two-mode case as the minimal genuinely coupled scenario.
AI.result: The first complete, certificate-checked solution for quantum complexity extraction in a genuinely coupled (two-mode) sector, with rigorous proof that the solution cannot be given in closed form.
AI.conclusion: Quantum complexity extraction from mixed Gaussian states in genuinely coupled modes is feasible but highly nontrivial, requiring certificate-checked methods and lacking closed-form solutions even in the simplest two-mode case.

title: Active Learning for Calibrating Entangling Gates via Surrogate-Based Optimization
summary: The fidelity of a quantum gate is sensitive to small deviations in the physical control parameters. Unfortunately, it is generally difficult to exactly model the implemented Hamiltonian for a set of user-defined parameters, necessitating on-device calibration. Here, we present an active learning framework based on Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian Process surrogate to find the optimal parameter set. We validate the technique through numerical calibration of the laser amplitude and frequencies that implement the trapped-ion Mølmer Sørensen gate. We show that a Gaussian process can model the Hamiltonian dynamics. The addition of active learning accelerates the discovery of the optimal parameter set with speed and final fidelity dependent on the quantum projection noise of the data. These results establish the utility of active learning and surrogate models for quantum calibration and control.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an active learning framework using Bayesian optimization with Gaussian Process surrogates to calibrate quantum gates, demonstrated on trapped-ion Mølmer-Sørensen gates, showing accelerated discovery of optimal parameters with fidelity dependent on quantum projection noise.
AI.motivation: Quantum gate fidelity is sensitive to small deviations in physical control parameters, and it is difficult to exactly model the implemented Hamiltonian for user-defined parameters, necessitating on-device calibration.
AI.method: An active learning framework based on Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian Process surrogate model to find the optimal parameter set.
AI.result: The technique is validated through numerical calibration of laser amplitude and frequencies for trapped-ion Mølmer-Sørensen gates. A Gaussian process can model Hamiltonian dynamics, and active learning accelerates optimal parameter discovery, with speed and final fidelity dependent on quantum projection noise.
AI.conclusion: These results establish the utility of active learning and surrogate models for quantum calibration and control.

title: Scattering, bound states, and resonances in the one-dimensional Dirac equation via supersymmetric quantum mechanics
summary: We develop a unified treatment of scattering and discrete spectra for the one-dimensional Dirac equation with scalar and vector interactions. Under the spin-symmetry condition, the coupled first-order Dirac system maps exactly onto an effective Sturm--Liouville (Schrö\-din\-ger-like) problem for a single spinor component. This mapping provides a convenient framework for analyzing transmission, reflection, and analytic continuation. As an explicit application, we consider effective interactions of hyperbolic Pöschl--Teller type and exploit supersymmetric quantum mechanics and shape invariance to obtain a closed-form expression for the transmission probability. The bound-state spectrum is then recovered from the poles of the analytically continued transmission amplitude, reproducing known results and offering a unified description of scattering and bound states. For the barrier configuration, we briefly comment on the resulting pole pattern in the complex momentum plane and its connection with resonance and quasi-normal-mode behavior. Moreover, we use the chiral transformation to relate the spin- and pseudospin-symmetry sectors and translate results between them without repeating the full derivation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified framework for solving the one-dimensional Dirac equation with scalar and vector interactions, mapping it to a Sturm–Liouville problem under spin symmetry. Using hyperbolic Pöschl–Teller potentials and supersymmetric quantum mechanics, closed-form transmission probabilities are derived, and bound states emerge from pole analysis of the scattering amplitude. Chiral transformations connect spin- and pseudospin-symmetry sectors.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified treatment of scattering and bound states for the one-dimensional Dirac equation with both scalar and vector interactions, bridging the gap between discrete and continuous spectral analyses.
AI.method: The coupled Dirac system is mapped onto an effective Sturm–Liouville (Schrödinger-like) problem under the spin-symmetry condition. Supersymmetric quantum mechanics and shape invariance are applied to hyperbolic Pöschl–Teller interactions to derive closed-form transmission probabilities. Analytic continuation of the transmission amplitude recovers bound-state spectra. Chiral transformations relate spin- and pseudospin-symmetry sectors.
AI.result: Closed-form expression for transmission probability for hyperbolic Pöschl–Teller interactions; bound-state spectra recovered from poles of the analytically continued transmission amplitude; pole pattern in the complex momentum plane for barrier configurations linked to resonances and quasinormal modes.
AI.conclusion: The mapping provides a convenient, unified framework for analyzing both scattering and bound states in the one-dimensional Dirac equation, and chiral transformations allow translation of results between spin- and pseudospin-symmetry sectors without full re-derivation.

title: Coupling effect of nearest-neighbor interacting qubit chains to a single qubit system
summary: This study establishes a theorem that provides sufficient criteria for identifying terms in any time-independent Hamiltonian that have no influence on local dynamics, local observables, or any local phenomena, without any approximation. The usefulness of this theorem is demonstrated by predicting the behavior of three systems. The first system consists of multiple qubit chains with Ising interactions. The second system is formed by a single qubit chain, differentiated by the substitution of Dzyalonshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction for the last Ising interaction. The predictions were verified by analytically deriving the reduced dynamics of both systems. A third system was also considered, namely, a short qubit chain with a transverse magnetic field on the intermediary environment qubit. This transverse magnetic field signals that the commutation relation required by our theorem no longer holds. The third system's local dynamics were also derived analytically, demonstrating that all Hamiltonian constituents contributed to the reduced dynamics. The physical consequences of our theorem's inapplicability were also explored using this third system by analyzing the entanglement dynamics between the qubits that do not directly interact. The results showed that the entanglement is caused by an \textit{emergent coupling} between the two non-directly interacting subsystems. This \textit{emergent coupling} arises from the non-commutativity of the intermediate interactions connecting the two subsystems. When searching for these \textit{emergent couplings}, our theorem can eliminate intermediate interactions that will not produce them.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a theorem providing sufficient criteria to identify Hamiltonian terms that have no effect on local dynamics, local observables, or local phenomena. The theorem is verified analytically on three qubit systems: multiple Ising-interacting qubit chains; a qubit chain with a DM interaction substitution; and a short qubit chain with a transverse magnetic field that violates the theorem's commutation condition—revealing emergent couplings from non-commuting intermediate interactions.
AI.motivation: To develop a rigorous, approximation-free method for identifying Hamiltonian terms that are irrelevant to local physics, thereby simplifying analysis of quantum systems.
AI.method: A theorem is proven establishing sufficient criteria (based on commutation relations) for term irrelevance. Its predictions are tested by analytically deriving reduced dynamics for three qubit-chain systems with varying interaction structures.
AI.result: The theorem correctly identified irrelevant terms in the first two systems (Ising chains and DM-modified chain), verified by analytic reduced dynamics. In the third system (where the theorem is inapplicable due to a transverse field), all Hamiltonian terms contributed, and emergent entanglement between non-directly interacting qubits arose from non-commuting intermediate interactions.
AI.conclusion: The theorem provides a powerful, exact tool for identifying locally irrelevant Hamiltonian terms, and can help locate emergent couplings by ruling out intermediate interactions that cannot produce them.

title: Quantum advantage prediction in turbulent free-space quantum illumination
summary: Quantum illumination offers a significant theoretical advantage for target detection in high background noise environments. However, its practical deployment in free-space channels is hindered by atmospheric turbulence. Stochastic fluctuations in atmospheric turbulence inevitably degrade the quantum signature, rendering the real-time evaluation of quantum advantage under such dynamic conditions a critical yet unresolved challenge. To circumvent the reliance on costly direct turbulence measurements, we propose a physics-driven framework that integrates Kolmogorov-Arnold networks directly bridge macroscopic meteorological observations with microscopic quantum channel dynamics. Trained on 105,120 samples from 12 climatically diverse sites and validated on 26,280 unseen samples from three extreme boundary conditions (arid continental, tropical maritime, high-altitude plateau), our approach establishes a physically consistent mapping from standard meteorological variables to the temporal evolution of the quantum advantage. This end-to-end system dynamically quantifies the degradation of quantum advantage across diverse turbulence conditions. Our results provide a rigorous theoretical and data-driven pathway for environmental adaptation, facilitating the transition of quantum radar networks from proof-of-principle demonstrations to all-weather operational systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a physics-driven framework using Kolmogorov-Arnold networks to infer quantum advantage degradation from standard meteorological data, bypassing direct turbulence measurements. Trained on 105,120 samples from 12 sites and validated on 26,280 samples from 3 extreme boundary conditions, it establishes a mapping from meteorological variables to quantum advantage dynamics under atmospheric turbulence, enabling all-weather quantum radar operations.
AI.motivation: The real-time evaluation of quantum advantage under dynamic atmospheric turbulence is a critical yet unresolved challenge, and direct turbulence measurements are costly. The authors aim to circumvent this by using standard meteorological observations to infer quantum channel dynamics.
AI.method: A physics-driven framework integrating Kolmogorov-Arnold networks that bridges macroscopic meteorological observations with microscopic quantum channel dynamics. The model is trained on 105,120 samples from 12 climatically diverse sites and validated on 26,280 unseen samples from three extreme boundary conditions (arid continental, tropical maritime, high-altitude plateau).
AI.result: The framework establishes a physically consistent mapping from standard meteorological variables to the temporal evolution of quantum advantage, dynamically quantifying its degradation across diverse turbulence conditions.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a rigorous theoretical and data-driven pathway for environmental adaptation, facilitating the transition of quantum radar networks from proof-of-principle demonstrations to all-weather operational systems.

title: Wallis Products from the Four-Dimensional Singular Harmonic Oscillator
summary: We present a variational derivation of the Wallis product and its reciprocal from the four-dimensional singular harmonic oscillator. The inverse-square interaction is absorbed into an effective angular parameter $ν$, so that the lowest exact energy in a fixed sector is $E_{4d,\mathrm{exact}}=\hbarω(ν+2)$. Motivated by the radial Kustaanheimo--Stiefel relation $r=ρ^2$ between the four-dimensional oscillator and the three-dimensional Coulomb problem, we use the quartic trial family $R_a(ρ)=Nρ^νe^{-aρ^4}$. The minimized variational energy yields an accuracy ratio governed by adjacent Gamma functions. In the large-$ν$ semiclassical limit, this ratio approaches unity. Restricting $ν$ to the odd sequence $ν=2n-1$ gives the standard Wallis product, whereas the even sequence $ν=2n$ gives its reciprocal form. The Coulomb-dual interpretation further relates the two branches to integer and half-integer effective angular sectors in the dual Coulomb/MICZ description. The result shows that Wallis-type infinite products persist under an inverse-square deformation of the oscillator and arise from a common Gamma-function structure in radial variational dynamics.

AI.tldr: A variational derivation of the Wallis product and its reciprocal from the four-dimensional singular harmonic oscillator with inverse-square interaction is presented. Using a quartic trial wavefunction and the radial Kustaanheimo-Stiefel relation, the minimized variational energy yields accuracy ratios governed by Gamma functions. Odd and even effective angular parameter sequences produce the standard and reciprocal Wallis products respectively, with Coulomb-dual interpretation linking to integer/half-integer angular sectors.
AI.motivation: To derive Wallis-type products variationally from a four-dimensional singular harmonic oscillator with inverse-square interactions, using the radial Kustaanheimo-Stiefel relation connecting the 4D oscillator to the 3D Coulomb problem.
AI.method: Variational approach with quartic trial wavefunction R_a(ρ)=Nρ^ν e^{-aρ^4}, where the inverse-square interaction is absorbed into an effective angular parameter ν. The minimized variational energy yields accuracy ratios governed by adjacent Gamma functions, and restriction to odd (ν=2n-1) and even (ν=2n) sequences yields the standard and reciprocal Wallis products.
AI.result: The large-ν semiclassical limit yields an accuracy ratio approaching unity. Odd ν=2n-1 gives the standard Wallis product; even ν=2n gives its reciprocal form. Coulomb-dual interpretation links the two branches to integer and half-integer effective angular sectors.
AI.conclusion: Wallis-type infinite products persist under inverse-square deformation of the oscillator and arise from a common Gamma-function structure in radial variational dynamics.

title: Extreme volume monogamy via bound-state engineering
summary: Quantum steering ellipsoid (QSE) provides a faithful representation of a two-qubit state. When extended to tripartite systems, the steerability from a trusted party to different receivers is subject to volume monogamy relations, which only constrain the total steerability but cannot individually eliminate the steerability of an untrusted third party, leaving a potential channel for information leakage via steering. Here, we show that this residual steerability can be completely suppressed by selectively engineering bound states in local qubit-environment subsystems, without compromising the steerability between trusted parties. Specifically, when bound states are formed in the subsystems formed by the trusted parties and their environments but absent in the untrusted one, the untrusted party's QSE volume decays to zero, while the trusted party's QSE volume remains finite. Our results establish selective bound-state engineering as a mechanism for extreme volume monogamy, with potential applications in secure quantum communication with an untrusted third party.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that by selectively engineering bound states in local qubit-environment subsystems, the residual quantum steering ellipsoid (QSE) volume of an untrusted third party can be suppressed to zero while preserving finite steerability between trusted parties, achieving extreme volume monogamy for secure quantum communication.
AI.motivation: Existing volume monogamy relations for tripartite quantum steering only constrain total steerability but cannot individually eliminate the steerability of an untrusted third party, leaving a potential channel for information leakage via steering. The authors aim to completely suppress this residual steerability.
AI.method: The authors propose selective bound-state engineering in local qubit-environment subsystems. Bound states are formed in subsystems of trusted parties and their environments but are absent in the untrusted party's subsystem, causing the untrusted party's QSE volume to decay to zero while the trusted party's QSE volume remains finite.
AI.result: When bound states are selectively formed in trusted parties' subsystems but absent in the untrusted one, the untrusted party's quantum steering ellipsoid volume decays to zero, while the trusted party's QSE volume remains finite.
AI.conclusion: Selective bound-state engineering serves as a mechanism for extreme volume monogamy in quantum steering ellipsoids, with potential applications in secure quantum communication involving an untrusted third party.

title: When AI meets quantum information: A comprehensive review
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum information (QI) are rapidly co-evolving. AI is becoming a practical tool for learning, designing, controlling, and verifying quantum systems, while QI offers new computational models, representational structures, and learning-theoretic questions for AI. This survey reviews the interface from both directions. In the AI for QI direction, we organize recent progress around the central tasks of extracting information from limited measurements, training and discovering quantum algorithms, stabilizing noisy hardware, automating experimental and programming workflows, and extending learning-based methods to sensing and networking. In the QI for AI direction, we examine how quantum computation and quantum-inspired structures affect learning through algorithmic speedups, expressivity, trainability, generalization, neural-network design, and tensor-network representations. We close by identifying cross-cutting challenges in reproducibility, scalability, hardware realism, and co-design, arguing that progress will depend on tighter integration of theory, experiment, and hybrid quantum--classical systems.

AI.tldr: This survey comprehensively reviews the bidirectional relationship between AI and quantum information, covering AI techniques for quantum systems (measurement, algorithm discovery, hardware stabilization, automation, sensing/networking) and quantum-inspired methods for AI (algorithmic speedups, expressivity, trainability, neural network design, tensor networks), while identifying cross-cutting challenges in reproducibility, scalability, hardware realism, and co-design.
AI.motivation: AI and quantum information are rapidly co-evolving, yet their intersection lacks a unified treatment; this survey aims to organize the fragmented progress from both directions to provide a coherent overview and identify key challenges.
AI.method: The paper systematically reviews the literature along two axes: (1) AI for QI — covering measurement extraction, quantum algorithm discovery, hardware noise stabilization, experimental/programming automation, and sensing/networking; (2) QI for AI — covering algorithmic speedups, expressivity, trainability, generalization, neural-network design, and tensor-network representations.
AI.result: The survey organizes recent progress into structured categories for both directions and identifies cross-cutting challenges: reproducibility, scalability, hardware realism, and co-design of hybrid quantum-classical systems.
AI.conclusion: Progress at the AI–QI interface will depend on tighter integration of theory, experiment, and hybrid quantum–classical systems, requiring coordinated efforts to address reproducibility, scalability, and hardware-realistic co-design.

title: Subsystem Thermalization and Work Statistical Characterizations of Floquet Dynamics
summary: We study Floquet thermalization in a periodically driven quantum non-integrable Ising chain by combining two operational diagnostics: subsystem thermalization and work statistics. For generic interacting Floquet systems, stroboscopic dynamics lead to heating toward an infinite-temperature state at low driving frequencies, to a prethermal state during the crossover regime, and then to a finite-temperature state at high driving frequencies. We show that reduced density matrices of small subsystems provide a precise measure of local equilibration and clearly resolve prethermal plateaus. In parallel, we analyze the statistics of work performed over a Floquet cycle using both the characteristic function of work with and without the two-point measurements, and the related fluctuation theorem, which captures coherent contributions and deviations from thermal equilibrium. By comparing these two diagnostics within the same Floquet setting, we demonstrate that work statistics encode the same dynamical crossover that governs subsystem thermalization. Our results establish a unified and experimentally accessible framework for characterizing Floquet thermalization, prethermal regimes, and coherent energy absorption in interacting quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Floquet thermalization in a driven quantum Ising chain, showing that subsystem thermalization and work statistics both capture the same dynamical crossover from heating to infinite-temperature (low frequency), through prethermal plateaus, to finite-temperature states (high frequency), establishing a unified framework for characterizing Floquet thermalization.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified and experimentally accessible framework for characterizing Floquet thermalization, prethermal regimes, and coherent energy absorption in interacting quantum systems by combining two operational diagnostics.
AI.method: Combining two diagnostics: (1) subsystem thermalization via reduced density matrices of small subsystems to measure local equilibration and resolve prethermal plateaus; (2) work statistics using the characteristic function with and without two-point measurements and the related fluctuation theorem.
AI.result: Both diagnostics capture the same dynamical crossover: subsystem thermalization and work statistics equivalently encode the transition from heating to infinite-temperature states (low driving frequency), prethermal plateaus (crossover regime), and finite-temperature states (high driving frequency).
AI.conclusion: Work statistics and subsystem thermalization provide a unified framework for characterizing Floquet thermalization, prethermalization, and coherent energy absorption in driven quantum systems.

title: Closed-loop control for two-qubit gates with trapped ions
summary: State-of-the-art two-qubit gates with trapped ions employ open-loop control that rely on simplified models to precompute control sequences. Our aim is to introduce closed-loop control for two-qubit gates to correct disturbances as they occur during the gate implementation. We introduce a spectator ion into the ion chain used for quantum logic processing, where it couples with the other ions through collective motional modes. The spectator ion's position is continuously monitored by driving dipole transitions and detecting the resultant fluorescence. We show that incorporating a spectator ion is feasible for linear Paul trap implementations and is expected to reduce the two-qubit gate Bell-state preparation infidelity by an order of magnitude with the deleterious effects of position monitoring being negligible compared to the thermal effects that exist in the system, even in the absence of the spectator ions. Mathematically, we describe driven ion-trap dynamics, including the spectator ion, by a stochastic quantum master equation involving the amplitude-modulation multimode-motional coupling gate, motional drift, thermal effects, recoil from photon scattering, spontaneous decay, and light shift. Our on-the-fly control method employs reinforcement learning with the reward function based on the actual geometric phase of the spectator ion. A key advantage of our approach is that we introduce a control method that involves `learning' and correcting disturbances happening in the trap on-the-fly, thus achieving high-fidelity gates. Our approach will lead to a significantly higher two-qubit gate fidelity at a reduced calibration overhead owing to the small parameter drift in the control system.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a closed-loop control method for two-qubit gates in trapped ions using a spectator ion and reinforcement learning, which continuously monitors and corrects disturbances during gate implementation, reducing Bell-state infidelity by an order of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art two-qubit gates with trapped ions use open-loop control based on simplified models, which cannot correct disturbances as they occur during gate implementation. The authors aim to introduce closed-loop control to dynamically correct these disturbances.
AI.method: A spectator ion is added to the ion chain and continuously monitored via dipole transition fluorescence. The system dynamics are described by a stochastic quantum master equation accounting for amplitude-modulation multimode-motional coupling, drift, thermal effects, recoil, decay, and light shift. Control is achieved via reinforcement learning with a reward function based on the spectator ion's geometric phase.
AI.result: Incorporating a spectator ion is feasible for linear Paul traps and is expected to reduce two-qubit gate Bell-state preparation infidelity by an order of magnitude. The deleterious effects of position monitoring are negligible compared to existing thermal effects, even without spectator ions.
AI.conclusion: This closed-loop control method achieves high-fidelity gates by learning and correcting disturbances on-the-fly, leading to significantly higher two-qubit gate fidelity with reduced calibration overhead due to small parameter drift in the control system.

title: Bridging quantum mechanics and nonlinear optics in Raman scattering
summary: We present a theoretical framework for spontaneous Raman scattering that fundamentally bridges quantum-mechanical and nonlinear-optical approaches. By conceptualizing spontaneous Raman scattering as a stimulated Raman gain or loss event seeded by the quantum vacuum field, we rigorously derive the spontaneous Raman cross-section directly from the third-order nonlinear susceptibility. Crucially, this framework predicts the existence of a hitherto unrecognized phenomenon: "spontaneous Raman loss" (sRL), which acts as the vacuum-seeded counterpart to stimulated Raman loss, complementing traditional spontaneous Raman scattering (spontaneous Raman gain, sRG). Furthermore, we establish a rigorous connection to the traditional Kramers-Heisenberg-Dirac (KHD) theory, revealing that the spontaneous process is governed by interference before a detector between the signal field emitted from molecules and the vacuum field itself that stimulates the molecules. This insight uncovers a direct correspondence between the sRG susceptibility and the rotating/counter-rotating interference terms in the KHD formula. Ultimately, we extend the foundational KHD theory by incorporating previously unrecognized essential terms, achieving perfect analytical agreement between the quantum mechanical and nonlinear optical descriptions of Raman scattering.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a theoretical framework unifying quantum-mechanical and nonlinear-optical descriptions of spontaneous Raman scattering, revealing that spontaneous Raman scattering is a stimulated process seeded by the quantum vacuum. It predicts a new phenomenon called "spontaneous Raman loss" (sRL) as the vacuum-seeded counterpart to stimulated Raman loss, and extends Kramers-Heisenberg-Dirac (KHD) theory by incorporating previously missing terms to achieve perfect agreement between the two approaches.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to bridge the gap between quantum-mechanical and nonlinear-optical approaches to spontaneous Raman scattering, and to resolve inconsistencies between the Kramers-Heisenberg-Dirac theory and nonlinear-optical descriptions.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize spontaneous Raman scattering as a stimulated Raman gain or loss event seeded by the quantum vacuum field. They derive the spontaneous Raman cross-section directly from the third-order nonlinear susceptibility and establish a rigorous connection to traditional KHD theory by analyzing interference between the signal field emitted from molecules and the vacuum field.
AI.result: The framework predicts a new phenomenon: "spontaneous Raman loss" (sRL), which is the vacuum-seeded counterpart to stimulated Raman loss. It also uncovers a direct correspondence between the sRG susceptibility and rotating/counter-rotating interference terms in the KHD formula, and successfully extends KHD theory by incorporating previously unrecognized essential terms.
AI.conclusion: The extended KHD theory achieves perfect analytical agreement between quantum mechanical and nonlinear optical descriptions of Raman scattering, fundamentally unifying these two previously disparate approaches.

title: Dependency-Aware Circuit Scheduling for Multi-Core Quantum Systems to Minimize Makespan
summary: Multi-core quantum computing architectures have emerged as a promising solution to the qubit scalability limitations of monolithic NISQ devices. Quantum algorithms are expressed as quantum circuits composed of single- and two-qubit gates. However, circuit scheduling in multi-core quantum systems remains largely unexplored. Reducing overall execution time (makespan), increasing core utilization, and hiding communication latency behind computation depends on effective scheduling. In this paper, we first introduce a layered scheduling approach as a baseline where quantum gates within the same layer are executed in parallel, while layers themselves are executed sequentially. We then propose a greedy scheduling strategy which schedules each gate as soon as all its dependencies and required resources are available. This allows fine-grained parallelism across cores. Our evaluation shows that on real benchmarks, greedy scheduling achieves an average 40% reduction in makespan and improvement in core utilization. The results suggest that the use of intelligent circuit scheduling to exploit parallelism can greatly enhance the speed of circuit execution in multi-core quantum architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a greedy scheduling strategy for multi-core quantum computing architectures that achieves a 40% reduction in makespan and improved core utilization compared to a layered baseline approach, demonstrating that intelligent circuit scheduling can significantly enhance execution speed.
