title: Conditional Enhancement of Dissipation-Induced Nonreciprocity by Quantum Squeezing
summary: We systematically investigate the role of squeezing in improving dissipation-induced nonreciprocal coupling mediated by a common reservoir, by incorporating a $χ^{(2)}$ nonlinearity into either the cavity mode, the reservoir, or both. Squeezing is capable of exponentially enhancing the effective coupling, but this enhancement is not universal in such a nonreciprocal interaction. Instead, it depends on the system configuration and specific parameter regimes. Specifically, the squeezing of the reservoir injects additional energy into the system via the dissipation channel, modifying the underlying dynamics in a nontrivial manner. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed approach enhances the performance of the quantum battery, including stored energy, charging power, and ergotropy. We provide the corresponding analytical expressions, together with a systematic analysis of energy transport and parameter optimization. Extending the framework to optical isolation, we observe an exponentially amplified output signal. Our results open a new avenue for nonreciprocal quantum information processing and nonreciprocal quantum device design.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how squeezing (via χ(2) nonlinearity) enhances dissipation-induced nonreciprocal coupling. Squeezing can exponentially boost effective coupling, but enhancement depends on configuration and parameter regimes. Reservoir squeezing injects energy via dissipation, modifying dynamics. The approach improves quantum battery performance (stored energy, charging power, ergotropy) and enables exponentially amplified optical isolation.
AI.motivation: To systematically explore the role of squeezing in enhancing dissipation-induced nonreciprocal coupling mediated by a common reservoir, and to understand its parameter-dependent behavior beyond universal enhancement assumptions.
AI.method: Incorporating χ(2) nonlinearity into either the cavity mode, the reservoir, or both; deriving analytical expressions for coupling enhancement; analyzing energy transport and parameter optimization across different system configurations.
AI.result: Squeezing exponentially enhances effective nonreciprocal coupling, but the enhancement is configuration-dependent and not universal. Reservoir squeezing injects energy nontrivially via dissipation. The approach improves quantum battery metrics (stored energy, charging power, ergotropy) and yields exponentially amplified output signals in optical isolation.
AI.conclusion: The work opens new avenues for nonreciprocal quantum information processing and nonreciprocal quantum device design.

title: Experimental Quantification of Layered Error Suppression in Fiber-Interconnected Quantum Data Centers
comment: Accepted as Oral Presenation in ECOC 2026, European Conference on Optical Communication
summary: We perform experiments to quantify error suppression in fiber-connected superconducting QPUs using combined error mitigation techniques, demonstrating over 20\% improvement in operational fidelity across interconnected quantum processing units under realistic noise conditions.

AI.tldr: Experiments show >20% fidelity improvement in fiber-connected superconducting QPUs via combined error mitigation under realistic noise.
AI.motivation: To quantify error suppression in distributed (fiber-connected) superconducting QPUs, which face additional noise from interconnects, and demonstrate practical benefits of combined error mitigation.
AI.method: Experimental benchmarking on fiber-linked superconducting quantum processors; application of multiple error mitigation techniques in combination; measurement of operational fidelity under realistic noise conditions.
AI.result: Over 20% improvement in operational fidelity across interconnected quantum processing units.
AI.conclusion: Combined error mitigation techniques effectively suppress errors in distributed quantum systems, enabling more reliable multi-chip quantum computing.

title: Asymmetric Light Scattering from an Atomic System with Gain: A Quantum Analysis
summary: We study the the scattering of light by a binary system of identical atoms in which one of them is incoherently pumped. This system belongs to the kind of non-parity symmetric optical systems in which gains and losses are partially compensated. We carry out a fully quantum analysis of the directionality of the radiation scattered from the atoms when the incident light strikes the system either perpendicular or alongside the interatomic axis. We find that, generally, while the degree of asymmetry depends on the pump rate, the preferred direction for emission depends on the interatomic distance and the detuning of the probe field with respect to the resonant frequency. On physical grounds, for the case of frontal illumination, the asymmetry is the result of the interference of the photons emitted from different atoms. On the contrary, for side lighting, the asymmetry with respect to the side of incidence is caused by both the phase difference between the probe field photons that strike each atom and the interference between the photons emitted from different atoms. Further, for side lighting too, our quantum approach demonstrates that the forward scattered power depends on the side of incidence, which reveals the lack of reciprocity in the quantum optical response of the system. This result conflicts with what is obtained within a classical approach.

AI.tldr: This paper studies light scattering by a binary system of identical atoms with one incoherently pumped, revealing asymmetric emission directionality due to quantum interference effects, and demonstrating non-reciprocal forward scattering in side lighting that contradicts classical predictions.
AI.motivation: To understand the directionality and asymmetry of scattered radiation in non-parity symmetric optical systems with partial gain-loss compensation, using a fully quantum analysis.
AI.method: Fully quantum analysis of a binary system of identical atoms with one atom incoherently pumped, studying scattering under perpendicular (frontal) and alongside (side) illumination relative to the interatomic axis.
AI.result: Asymmetry degree depends on pump rate; preferred emission direction depends on interatomic distance and probe detuning. For frontal illumination, asymmetry arises from interference of photons from different atoms. For side lighting, asymmetry arises from both phase difference in probe photons striking each atom and photon interference. Side lighting also shows non-reciprocal forward scattered power depending on incidence side, contradicting classical approach predictions.
AI.conclusion: The quantum optical response of the system exhibits lack of reciprocity for side illumination, which cannot be captured by classical approaches, highlighting the importance of fully quantum treatment in such non-parity symmetric systems.

title: Bias-Preserving Gates and Quantum Error Correction With Dual-Rail Cat Codes
summary: Scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation requires quantum error-correcting codes that simultaneously support universal logical operations, suppress hardware-specific noise, and enable efficient handling of photon-loss errors. Bosonic encodings such as the dual-rail and cat codes each offer attractive features but also exhibit important limitations when used in isolation. The dual-rail code enables efficient single-photon-loss detection by converting leakage out of the computational subspace induced by photon-loss errors into an erasure error. In contrast, the cat code provides a resource-efficient, bias-tailored error-correction scheme with bias-preserving logical gate operations. Here, we introduce the dual-rail cat code (DRCC), a concatenated bosonic encoding that combines an inner cat code with an outer dual-rail structure, thereby inheriting and enhancing the advantages of both constituent codes. We analyse the error-correction properties of the DRCC and propose a deterministic single-photon-loss correction protocol by concatenating it with an outer repetition code. Exploiting the code's intrinsic noise bias, we construct a universal set of logical gates using only beam-splitter interactions and demonstrate that all logical operations preserve the erasure-biased noise structure. The DRCC offers several distinctive advantages, including the absence of relative geometric phases during gate operations, deterministic erasure detection and correction, and simultaneous syndrome extraction without interrupting stabilisation. These features make the DRCC a promising bosonic code for hardware-efficient, bias-preserving, and erasure-resilient fault-tolerant quantum computation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the dual-rail cat code (DRCC), a concatenated bosonic encoding combining an inner cat code with an outer dual-rail structure, which enables deterministic single-photon-loss correction, bias-preserving logical gates, and erasure-resilient fault-tolerant quantum computation.
AI.motivation: Existing bosonic encodings like dual-rail and cat codes each have attractive features but individual limitations (e.g., dual-rail enables efficient photon-loss detection but limited bias handling; cat code offers bias-tailored error correction but lacks efficient erasure handling). The authors aim to combine both to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: The DRCC concatenates an inner cat code with an outer dual-rail structure. The paper proposes a deterministic single-photon-loss correction protocol by further concatenating with an outer repetition code. Universal logical gates are constructed using only beam-splitter interactions, preserving erasure-biased noise.
AI.result: The DRCC provides: (1) absence of relative geometric phases during gate operations, (2) deterministic erasure detection and correction, (3) simultaneous syndrome extraction without interrupting stabilisation, and (4) bias-preserving logical gate operations.
AI.conclusion: The DRCC is a promising bosonic code for hardware-efficient, bias-preserving, and erasure-resilient fault-tolerant quantum computation, inheriting and enhancing the advantages of both dual-rail and cat codes.

title: Three-qubit nonlocality paradoxes: beyond GHZ
comment: Preliminary draft version; updated exposition forthcoming
summary:
Quantum nonlocality paradoxes, such as that of GHZ, provide maximally sharp logical obstructions to classical probabilistic models of quantum correlations. They are key resources in a broad variety of information-theoretic tasks that exhibit unconditional quantum advantage. For example, in nonlocal games, which are communication tasks that serve as core technical tools in recent landmark results in quantum computational complexity theory.
  Their role in establishing quantum advantage motivated their study by Abramsky et al. who introduced an infinite family of three-qubit paradoxes exhibiting novel conditional structure. This was later extended by de Silva et al. into a full classification program.
  In this work, we completely classify all three-qubit nonlocality paradoxes established via a biconditional parity proof; this is a very large class of paradoxes that encompasses all earlier-known examples. We do this by introducing a suite of new structural and combinatorial techniques. We find that the landscape of nonlocality paradoxes is far richer than previously understood, violating regularity conditions underlying all prior constructions.

AI.tldr: This paper completely classifies all three-qubit nonlocality paradoxes established via biconditional parity proof, introducing new structural and combinatorial techniques that reveal a richer landscape of paradoxes than previously known, violating regularity conditions underlying all prior constructions.
AI.motivation: Quantum nonlocality paradoxes are key resources for tasks exhibiting unconditional quantum advantage, motivating the need for a systematic classification, especially after Abramsky et al. introduced an infinite family of three-qubit paradoxes and de Silva et al. initiated a classification program.
AI.method: The authors completely classify all three-qubit nonlocality paradoxes established via biconditional parity proof using a suite of new structural and combinatorial techniques.
AI.result: The landscape of nonlocality paradoxes is far richer than previously understood, violating regularity conditions underlying all prior constructions. The classification encompasses all earlier-known examples.
AI.conclusion: The complete classification of three-qubit nonlocality paradoxes via biconditional parity proofs reveals a significantly more diverse set of paradoxes than previously recognized, challenging prior assumptions about their structure.

title: Hierarchy of hidden nonlocality: A genuine activation of Incompletability
summary: Quantum nonlocality admits several operational manifestations, one of which emerges from sets of orthogonal quantum states that cannot be perfectly distinguished by local operations and classical communication (LOCC). Such sets are regarded as nonlocal because their perfect discrimination requires global measurements. In contrast, sets that are perfectly distinguishable by LOCC are generally considered locally accessible and operationally classical. In this work, we investigate the role of incompletability in local state discrimination and introduce the notion of \emph{activation of incompletability}. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of orthogonal sets that are initially perfectly distinguishable by LOCC and free from local redundancy, but which can be transformed via LOCC into strictly incompletable sets. We prove that activation of incompletability necessarily implies activation of nonlocality, whereas the converse fails in general, thereby establishing a hierarchy between the two activation phenomena. Furthermore, within the framework of local incoherent operations and classical communication (LICC), we show that any set whose incompletability can be activated can nevertheless be extended to a complete orthonormal basis of the Hilbert space, although the resulting completed basis is no longer perfectly distinguishable by LOCC. Our results uncover a fundamental interplay among local distinguishability, incompletability, coherence, and nonlocality, and provide new insight into the structure of locally accessible quantum information.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the concept of "activation of incompletability" in quantum nonlocality, showing that certain orthogonal quantum sets initially perfectly distinguishable by LOCC can be transformed into strictly incompletable sets, revealing a hierarchy between activation of incompletability and activation of nonlocality.
AI.motivation: To investigate the role of incompletability in local state discrimination and establish a fundamental connection between incompletability, nonlocality, coherence, and local distinguishability of quantum states.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate existence of orthogonal sets perfectly distinguishable by LOCC but transformable into incompletable sets via LOCC. They prove a hierarchy (activation of incompletability implies activation of nonlocality, but not vice versa) and analyze the framework of local incoherent operations and classical communication (LICC).
AI.result: - Existence of orthogonal sets that are LOCC-distinguishable and free from local redundancy but can be activated into strictly incompletable sets. - Activation of incompletability necessarily implies activation of nonlocality, but the converse fails. - Under LICC, activated incompletable sets can still be extended to a complete orthonormal basis, but the completed basis is no longer LOCC-distinguishable.
AI.conclusion: The results uncover fundamental interplay among local distinguishability, incompletability, coherence, and nonlocality, providing new insights into the structure of locally accessible quantum information.

title: Synthesizing Compound Pulse Gadgets for Hamiltonian Simulation on Trapped-Ion Platforms
comment: Presented at The Fifth International Workshop on Quantum Classical Cooperative Computing (QCCC-26). 5 pages, 3 figures
summary: Standard gate-level transpilation introduces significant physical noise and overhead for high-precision quantum algorithms, such as the Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT), on near-term trapped-ion hardware. Current compilers treat quantum operations as discrete units, forcing the physical control layer to execute highly fragmented laser pulses. To address this hardware-software disconnect, this work introduces a holistic pulse synthesis strategy that bypasses discrete gate-stitching to compile algorithms directly into continuous compound pulse gadgets. As a proof-of-concept, we target Hamiltonian simulation of the $H_2$ molecule, block-encoding the problem into a QSVT circuit to approximate the time-evolution operator $U = e^{-i H t}$ across 3 computational ions (2 system, 1 ancilla). We utilize the Gradient Ascent Pulse Engineering (GRAPE) algorithm to generate these compound gadgets and evaluate our methodology using noisy Lindblad master equation simulations. Preliminary observations indicate that the proposed strategy achieves significant temporal compression, reducing the total pulse schedule duration compared to standard compilers. Furthermore, synthesizing operations holistically eliminates the control-layer latency associated with discrete pulse lookup overhead. By streamlining the physical control schedule, this methodology offers a promising pathway to execute operations faster, highlighting the potential for compound gadgets to increase the computational depth achievable within fundamental $T_2$ decoherence limits.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a holistic pulse synthesis strategy that bypasses discrete gate-stitching to compile QSVT algorithms directly into continuous compound pulse gadgets, demonstrating temporal compression and reduced control-layer latency on trapped-ion hardware for H₂ molecule Hamiltonian simulation.
AI.motivation: Standard gate-level transpilation introduces significant physical noise and overhead for high-precision quantum algorithms like QSVT on near-term trapped-ion hardware, and current compilers force fragmented laser pulses due to treating quantum operations as discrete units, creating a hardware-software disconnect.
AI.method: The authors bypass discrete gate-stitching by compiling QSVT circuits directly into continuous compound pulse gadgets, using the GRAPE algorithm to generate these gadgets, and evaluate via noisy Lindblad master equation simulations on a 3-ion (2 system, 1 ancilla) trapped-ion system for H₂ Hamiltonian simulation.
AI.result: The proposed strategy achieves significant temporal compression—reducing total pulse schedule duration compared to standard compilers—and eliminates control-layer latency from discrete pulse lookup overhead, enabling faster operations within fundamental T₂ decoherence limits.
AI.conclusion: By streamlining the physical control schedule, compound pulse gadgets offer a promising pathway to increase computational depth achievable within T₂ decoherence limits on near-term trapped-ion hardware.

title: Simulating generic single-qubit open-dynamics via polarization-frequency coupling in a photonic interferometer
summary: We propose a photonic platform for simulating arbitrary single-qubit open-system dynamics using a single photon in an open Mach-Zehnder interferometer. A birefringent quartz plate induces a coupling between the polarization and frequency degrees of freedom. By treating the latter as an effective environment, we analytically derive the reduced polarization dynamics. We show that the resulting evolution is characterized by a controllable interplay between populations and coherence, instead of the usual dephasing caused by quartz plates. By adjusting the photon frequency distribution and interferometric parameters, we demonstrate that target single-qubit states can be efficiently reproduced through a tunable optical protocol expected to work under accessible experimental conditions. The simulator is benchmarked against paradigmatic open-system evolutions, including depolarization and non-Markovian dynamics, achieving high accuracy. Our results establish polarization-frequency engineered photonic interferometers as a versatile protocol for simulation of open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a photonic simulator using a single photon in an open Mach-Zehnder interferometer with a birefringent quartz plate to simulate arbitrary single-qubit open-system dynamics, achieving controllable population-coherence interplay and high-fidelity reproduction of target states under accessible experimental conditions.
AI.motivation: To develop a versatile photonic platform that can simulate arbitrary single-qubit open-system dynamics, addressing the need for controllable and experimentally accessible simulators for open quantum systems.
AI.method: A single photon in an open Mach-Zehnder interferometer with a birefringent quartz plate couples polarization (system) and frequency (environment) degrees of freedom. The reduced polarization dynamics are analytically derived, and the photon frequency distribution and interferometric parameters are tuned to control the evolution.
AI.result: The simulator achieves controllable interplay between populations and coherence, and is benchmarked against paradigmatic open-system evolutions (e.g., depolarization and non-Markovian dynamics) with high accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Polarization-frequency engineered photonic interferometers serve as a versatile and experimentally accessible protocol for simulating open quantum systems.

title: Twisted Gaussian Schell States in Quantum Optics: Twist-Assisted Nonclassicality and Entanglement
summary:
We introduce the Twisted Gaussian Schell (TGS) state, a two-mode mixed Gaussian state defined as the quantum-optical analog of the Twisted Gaussian Schell-model beam of classical paraxial optics, characterized by the so-called twist phase. In the TGS state, the twist parameter arises when an asymmetric two-mode thermal state is subject to local squeezing after the action of phase shifters and a beam splitter. Its defining quantum feature is nonclassicality: although the state is separable in its natural bipartition, when the twist parameter is nonzero there are global quadratures that can be squeezed below the shot-noise limit. The nonclassicality has also a direct signature in the joint photon-number distribution, which we obtain in closed form. Moreover, coupling each mode to an ancillary vacuum at a balanced beam splitter yields a four-mode state with entanglement in select $2\times2$ bipartitions, with local description given by two TGS states, and all $1\times3$ bipartitions.
  For fixed input squeezing, increasing the twist parameter activates entanglement where the state is otherwise separable and deepens it where already present. The classical physicality bound on the twist parameter coincides with the quantum physicality condition. These results advance the two-way bridge between classical beam engineering and quantum information.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Twisted Gaussian Schell (TGS) state, a two-mode mixed Gaussian state with a twist phase that exhibits nonclassicality (quadrature squeezing) and entanglement activated by the twist parameter, bridging classical beam engineering and quantum information.
AI.motivation: To define and analyze the TGS state as the quantum-optical analog of the classical Twisted Gaussian Schell-model beam, advancing the connection between classical beam engineering and quantum information processing.
AI.method: Analytical derivation: TGS state generated from an asymmetric two-mode thermal state via phase shifters, beam splitter, and local squeezing; analysis of quadrature squeezing, joint photon-number distribution, and entanglement in select bipartitions after coupling to ancillary vacua.
AI.result: TGS state is separable but nonclassical (quadrature squeezing below shot noise) for nonzero twist; closed-form joint photon-number distribution shows nonclassical signature; entanglement activated and deepened in 2x2 bipartitions as twist increases; classical and quantum physicality bounds coincide.
AI.conclusion: The TGS state bridges classical beam engineering and quantum information by demonstrating that twist phase induces nonclassicality and controllable entanglement, with classical physicality bound matching quantum physicality condition.

title: The Dynamical Lie Algebra of QAOA-MaxCut on the Complete Graph
summary: We give an analytical expression for the dynamical Lie algebra corresponding to the QAOA-MaxCut problem on complete graphs, and show that the variance of the associated loss function scales linearly in the number of qubits. This solves an open problem from [ASYZ26] and confirms that such systems do not exhibit barren plateaus. The proof is based on projecting the dynamical Lie algebra generators onto subspaces given by the Schur-Weyl duality between irreducible representations of the unitary and symmetric groups.

AI.tldr: The paper analytically derives the dynamical Lie algebra for QAOA-MaxCut on complete graphs, proves the loss function variance scales linearly with qubit count, confirming no barren plateaus, and solves an open problem using Schur-Weyl duality.
AI.motivation: To resolve an open problem from [ASYZ26] regarding whether QAOA-MaxCut on complete graphs exhibits barren plateaus, which is crucial for understanding trainability in quantum optimization.
AI.method: Projecting the dynamical Lie algebra generators onto subspaces defined by Schur-Weyl duality between irreducible representations of the unitary and symmetric groups.
AI.result: The dynamical Lie algebra has an analytical expression, and the variance of the loss function scales linearly in the number of qubits (not exponentially), confirming no barren plateaus.
AI.conclusion: The system does not exhibit barren plateaus, solving the open problem and providing theoretical guarantees for trainability of QAOA-MaxCut on complete graphs.

title: Bridging Quantum Computing Paradigms toward Semiconductor Yield: A Controlled CV-versus-DV Comparison on Wafer-Map Defect Classification
summary: Realizing quantum neural networks (QNNs) in industry requires knowing which quantum computing paradigm suits which task. Motivated by AI accelerators and high-bandwidth memory, where die stacking makes wafer-level defect screening central to yield, we study WM-811K wafer-map defect classification (eight classes), comparing the dominant paradigms, continuous-variable (CV) and discrete-variable (DV), under controlled conditions. To isolate the quantum circuit as the sole variable, a shared convolutional backbone (~4.3M parameters) feeds interchangeable heads (classical dense, CV-QNN, or DV-QNN) as the only structural difference; each quantum head is scaled over three sizes (3, 4, 8 qumodes/qubits). The CV head consistently outperforms the DV head: at four qumodes/qubits it reaches 79.7 +/- 1.8% accuracy versus 61.6 +/- 1.4%, a non-overlapping 18-point gap. The advantage is sharpest on the spatially localized Edge-Loc class, easily confused with Scratch, which CV recovers with recall 0.66 +/- 0.06 while DV fails at every size (<=0.05), showing the structured CV layer better captures fine spatial distinctions between defect types. Training curves show the DV limitation is a representational-capacity ceiling, not an optimization failure; at the Fock cutoff used here (d = 2) the CV advantage reflects two intrinsic properties, a structured, neural-network-analogue layer and continuous phase-space encoding, not Hilbert-space dimensionality. On IBM hardware, DV accuracy holds at shallow depth, degrading only at the deepest circuit. Both quantum heads remain below the classical baseline (85.0%), but the controlled setting isolates where a structured head already helps and, as noise and scale improve, which paradigm can deliver practical advantage.

AI.tldr: This paper compares continuous-variable (CV) and discrete-variable (DV) quantum neural network heads on WM-811K wafer defect classification, finding CV consistently outperforms DV (79.7% vs 61.6% accuracy at 4 qumodes/qubits) due to structured layer representation and continuous phase-space encoding, though both remain below the classical baseline (85.0%).
AI.motivation: To determine which quantum computing paradigm (CV vs DV) is better suited for wafer-map defect classification in semiconductor manufacturing, motivated by the need for wafer-level defect screening in die-stacked AI accelerators and high-bandwidth memory.
AI.method: A shared convolutional backbone (~4.3M parameters) feeds interchangeable heads (classical dense, CV-QNN, or DV-QNN) as the only structural difference, scaled over 3, 4, and 8 qumodes/qubits, tested on the WM-811K dataset (eight classes).
AI.result: CV head achieves 79.7±1.8% accuracy vs DV head's 61.6±1.4% at 4 qumodes/qubits (18-point gap); CV recall for Edge-Loc class is 0.66±0.06 vs DV ≤0.05; DV limitation is a representational-capacity ceiling, not optimization failure; DV accuracy holds on IBM hardware at shallow depth.
AI.conclusion: CV paradigm shows clear advantage over DV for wafer defect classification due to structured neural-network-analogue layers and continuous phase-space encoding; controlled setup isolates where a structured head helps, guiding which paradigm could deliver practical advantage as noise and scale improve.

title: Limitations of Error Model Approximations in Quantum Network Simulation
summary: Efficient classical simulation of large-scale quantum networks frequently relies on noise approximations, which consider a restricted set of operators to describe noisy channels and operations. In this work, we demonstrate how such simplified error models, such as Pauli twirling or reset channels, can lead to severe quantitative and qualitative discrepancies in protocol performance predictions. We analyze, in particular, how small differences can accumulate in iterative and sequential protocols such as entanglement purification, entanglement swapping, and repeater chains. Our results reveal that neglected error contributions can lead to important performance under- and over-estimations, measurement-outcome dependency, and oscillations in the fidelity, which are entirely overlooked by the simplified error model approximations. These results show that rigorous validation of complete noise architectures is indispensable for accurately predicting operational thresholds in future quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: Simplified noise models (e.g., Pauli twirling, reset channels) cause significant quantitative and qualitative errors in predicting performance of quantum network protocols like entanglement purification, swapping, and repeater chains, leading to fidelity oscillations and misestimated thresholds.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that commonly used noise approximations in classical simulation of quantum networks can produce severe discrepancies in performance predictions, and to highlight the need for rigorous validation of full noise architectures.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of simplified error models (Pauli twirling, reset channels) versus complete noise architectures in iterative and sequential quantum network protocols including entanglement purification, entanglement swapping, and repeater chains.
AI.result: Simplified noise models lead to performance under- and over-estimations, measurement-outcome dependency, and fidelity oscillations that are entirely missed by approximations; small errors accumulate significantly in iterative protocols.
AI.conclusion: Rigorous validation of complete noise architectures is indispensable for accurately predicting operational thresholds in future quantum technologies; simplified error models are insufficient for reliable predictions.

title: Analytical connection between exact and approximate solutions of the periodically-driven two-level system starting from the Heun equation
summary: We investigate and establish an analytic connection between the exact solutions describing the dynamics of a two-level system driven by periodic external fields, focusing on the cases of linear driving and the so-called rotating-wave approximation, or circular driving. In both cases, the exact solutions can be obtained by mapping the Schrodinger equation onto Heun equations: the confluent Heun equation for linear driving and the Heun equation for the rotating-wave case. In particular, we demonstrate a direct analytic connection between the exact solutions for linear driving and those for the rotating-wave case. This result is obtained by analyzing local solutions expressed in terms of hypergeometric functions, which, in the case of the confluent Heun equation, can be derived by considering path-multiplicative Floquet solutions involving a bilateral series. This series leads to two continued-fraction expansions that can be perturbatively solved by imposing a suitable consistency condition. The connection between the linear-driving and rotating-wave solutions is established through a perturbative procedure that allows us to recover not only the rotating-wave approximation itself, but also the correct Stark and Bloch-Siegert shifts, as well as the so-called high-frequency approximation.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes an analytic connection between exact solutions for two-level systems driven by periodic fields in linear driving (confluent Heun equation) and circular driving/rotating-wave approximation (Heun equation) cases, using hypergeometric local solutions, Floquet bilateral series, and continued-fraction expansions to recover the RWA, Stark/Bloch-Siegert shifts, and high-frequency approximation.
AI.motivation: To uncover the direct mathematical relationship between exact solutions of linear driving and rotating-wave approximation in two-level systems, bridging the gap between these two widely-studied driving regimes.
AI.method: Mapping the Schrödinger equation onto Heun equations (confluent for linear driving, standard for circular driving); analyzing local hypergeometric solutions; using path-multiplicative Floquet solutions with bilateral series; deriving continued-fraction expansions; imposing consistency conditions perturbatively.
AI.result: A direct analytic connection between linear-driving and rotating-wave solutions is demonstrated; the perturbative procedure recovers the RWA, correct Stark and Bloch-Siegert shifts, and the high-frequency approximation.
AI.conclusion: The two seemingly distinct driving regimes are analytically connected, allowing systematic recovery of standard approximations and shifts from a unified framework.

title: Susceptibility-kinetic uncertainty relations for quantum systems
summary: Kinetic uncertainty relations bound current precision of stochastic processes by dynamical activity. The extension of these bounds to quantum systems has been impeded by coherence, strong system-reservoir coupling, and the subtlety of defining dynamical activity in the quantum regime. Here, we introduce a partial dynamical activity through the quantum Fisher information associated with the rescaling of the system-reservoir coupling and show that it bounds current precision via a universal susceptibility-kinetic uncertainty relation. The general validity of this relation for any open quantum system is guaranteed by the natural contribution of a susceptibility term, which is experimentally accessible by tuning the system-reservoir coupling strength. We show how the partial dynamical activity encompasses previous definitions of activity in the weak-coupling Markovian limit and that it provides an information-geometric interpretation of correlator-based activities. We illustrate the tight constraint on precision that our bound provides with the example of steady-state transport through a double quantum dot, where quantum effects invalidate previously developed kinetic uncertainty relations. We expect our bound to provide a powerful tool for optimizing precision in arbitrary quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a universal susceptibility-kinetic uncertainty relation that bounds current precision in open quantum systems using a partial dynamical activity defined via quantum Fisher information, valid for any coupling strength and coherence regime.
AI.motivation: Kinetic uncertainty relations (KURs) bound current precision by dynamical activity in classical stochastic processes, but extending them to quantum systems is challenging due to coherence, strong system-reservoir coupling, and the difficulty of defining dynamical activity in the quantum regime.
AI.method: The authors define a partial dynamical activity using quantum Fisher information associated with rescaling system-reservoir coupling, deriving a susceptibility-kinetic uncertainty relation that includes a universal susceptibility term.
AI.result: The bound is universally valid for any open quantum system, encompasses previous definitions of activity in the weak-coupling Markovian limit, provides an information-geometric interpretation of correlator-based activities, and is tighter than previous KURs—demonstrated via steady-state transport through a double quantum dot where quantum effects invalidate earlier bounds.
AI.conclusion: The susceptibility-kinetic uncertainty relation offers a powerful tool for optimizing precision in arbitrary quantum systems, as its susceptibility term is experimentally accessible by tuning the system-reservoir coupling strength.

title: Optimizing Symmetry Informed Probabilistic Error Cancellation
summary: We show that combining quantum error detection (QED) with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) gives more accurate and lower-variance estimates than PEC alone, provided that the symmetry measurements required for QED are carefully chosen. Because noisy symmetry measurements can negate the benefits of the PEC+QED approach, we cast the selection of measurement configurations as a classical optimization problem that systematically suppresses the impact of noise. Applying optimized PEC+QED to GHZ-state output distributions and to simulating the time-dynamics of a generalized superfast encoded Fermi-Hubbard model, we find consistent improvements over PEC. For GHZ states, the optimization over symmetry measurement configurations is essential for achieving an advantage. For the Fermi-Hubbard model, PEC+QED improves observable estimation on a $2 \times 2$ lattice and for larger systems the mitigation overheads can be reduced by measuring only subsets of stabilizers. Our results demonstrate the importance of circuit-specific tailoring of QEM techniques and that fault-tolerant design principles may already provide value for near-term devices.

AI.tldr: Combining quantum error detection (QED) with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) improves accuracy and reduces variance compared to PEC alone, provided symmetry measurements are optimized to suppress noise. Applied to GHZ states and Fermi-Hubbard simulations, optimized PEC+QED consistently outperforms PEC, showing the value of circuit-specific quantum error mitigation (QEM) tailoring.
AI.motivation: Standard PEC suffers from high variance and limited accuracy in near-term quantum devices. The authors aim to enhance PEC by integrating QED's symmetry checks, but noisy symmetry measurements can degrade performance, motivating a systematic optimization of measurement configurations.
AI.method: The authors formulate the selection of symmetry measurement configurations as a classical optimization problem to minimize the impact of measurement noise. They apply the optimized PEC+QED approach to GHZ-state output distributions and time-dynamics simulations of a generalized superfast encoded Fermi-Hubbard model.
AI.result: Optimized PEC+QED consistently improves over PEC alone. For GHZ states, optimizing over symmetry measurement configurations was essential for advantage. For the Fermi-Hubbard model, improvements were seen on a 2×2 lattice, and mitigation overheads were reduced by measuring only subsets of stabilizers for larger systems.
AI.conclusion: Circuit-specific tailoring of QEM techniques is crucial. Fault-tolerant design principles, such as symmetry-based error detection, already provide value for near-term noisy quantum devices.

title: Fisher Glasses: Tail-Certified Quantum Metrology in Quenched Environments
summary: Quantum metrological advantage is certified by averaged Fisher responses: contrast, susceptibility, or quantum Fisher information (QFI). This fails in quenched sensors, where slow environmental variables freeze within a session but vary between repetitions: shallow nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, superconducting qubits with slow two-level fluctuators, and semiconductor spin qubits in drifting charge noise. They sample session-resolved Fisher geometries, not an averaged channel. Certification conditions on the latent session, projects nuisance directions, inverts to attainable loss, then tail-certifies; this inverse upper-tail loss defines quenched tail-certified information. A no-go theorem: no averaged Fisher data determine this certificate; ensembles sharing averaged Fisher matrix, QFI, and projected information have finite or zero certified precision. A Fisher-zero integrability transition governs collapse: the inverse-loss tail exponent $β$ sets the boundary, with nonintegrable certified loss for $β\le 1$, even when annealed information is large or scaling. The certified quantum resource is response transverse to latent disorder, not raw amplification sharing its generator; universal design laws: safe windows, nondegenerate portfolios, Fisher reserves, action separation, Fisher-cut criteria. A shallow-NV Ramsey tournament shows average-QFI optimization is tail-catastrophic, whereas tail-certified designs recover nearly three orders of magnitude in certified information at equal shot budget and latent ensemble. These non-self-averaging phases are Fisher glasses, governed by Fisher-zero rare-event statistics.

AI.tldr: Averaged Fisher information fails to certify quantum metrological advantage in quenched sensors due to session-resolved latent disorder. The authors propose "quenched tail-certified information" based on inverse upper-tail loss, governed by a Fisher-zero integrability transition with tail exponent β. Universal design laws (safe windows, nondegenerate portfolios, Fisher reserves, action separation, Fisher-cut criteria) are derived. A shallow-NV Ramsey tournament demonstrates that average-QFI optimization is tail-catastrophic, while tail-certified designs recover ~3 orders of magnitude in certified information.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum metrological certification using averaged Fisher responses (QFI, contrast, susceptibility) fails for quenched sensors where slow environmental variables freeze within a session but vary between repetitions. This applies to shallow NV centers, superconducting qubits with two-level fluctuators, and semiconductor spin qubits in drifting charge noise. A new certification framework is needed.
AI.method: The authors formulate session-resolved Fisher geometries, condition on the latent session, project nuisance directions, invert to obtain attainable loss, and tail-certify. They derive a no-go theorem showing averaged Fisher data cannot determine this certificate. A Fisher-zero integrability transition is identified, governed by the tail exponent β of the inverse-loss distribution. Universal design laws are derived from the certified quantum resource being response transverse to latent disorder.
AI.result: A no-go theorem: ensembles sharing the same averaged Fisher matrix, QFI, and projected information can have finite or zero certified precision. The tail exponent β sets the boundary: nonintegrable certified loss for β ≤ 1, even when annealed information is large or scaling. In a shallow-NV Ramsey tournament, average-QFI optimization is tail-catastrophic, while tail-certified designs recover nearly three orders of magnitude in certified information at equal shot budget and latent ensemble.
AI.conclusion: The certified quantum resource is response transverse to latent disorder, not raw amplification sharing its generator. Universal design laws include safe windows, nondegenerate portfolios, Fisher reserves, action separation, and Fisher-cut criteria. These non-self-averaging phases are termed "Fisher glasses," governed by Fisher-zero rare-event statistics. Average-QFI optimization can be catastrophically fragile under quenched disorder.

title: Entanglement-spectrum fingerprint of a non-invertible symmetry: the Kramers--Wannier duality defect on the lattice
summary: Non-invertible symmetries are characterized by topological defects of irrational quantum dimension, but their imprint on the entanglement of a quantum many-body state has not been resolved at the level of the spectrum. We show that the categorical data of the canonical example -- the Kramers--Wannier (KW) duality defect of the critical Ising chain, with quantum dimension d_sigma=sqrt(2) -- is encoded in the single-particle entanglement spectrum of its ground state: a maximally mixed Majorana zero mode is the spectral origin of the boundary entropy log g=(1/2)log 2, hence of d_sigma itself. Reading the same duality-twisted ground state along two independent routes -- the transfer-matrix momentum shift and the Casimir curvature of the energy -- pins the twist-field weight h_sigma=1/16 twice over, and the defect Hilbert space organizes into a half-integer sigma-twisted conformal tower. This promotes the boundary entropy from an integrated number to a level-resolved spectral signature of non-invertibility, and supplies an exactly solvable calibration target for tensor-network studies of duality defects that lack a free-fermion shortcut.

The defect Hilbert space organizes into half-integer σ-twisted conformal towers, with twist-field weight h_σ=1/16 confirmed via two independent methods.

title: Entanglement fingerprint of a non-invertible symmetry: exact Fibonacci cut charges on the lattice
summary: Non-invertible defects are usually diagnosed through scaling spectra or infrared CFT data. We show that the Fibonacci duality defect of the critical golden chain already carries an exact categorical fingerprint at finite lattice size. The even-length antiferromagnetic ground state has fixed cut-charge weights, giving P_tau/P_1=phi^2 and log g=log phi without finite-size extrapolation. The proof is a finite-dimensional operator identity for the sandwiched cut projectors, combined with a Perron-Frobenius sector theorem for the even-length ground state. This gives a sharp lattice-level boundary entropy for a non-Abelian duality defect. We also separate this exact two-charge result from the finer six-primary tricritical-Ising resolution: the latter is located by the standard scaling-limit Virasoro branching of A_4 affine-TL packets, and is not an assumption in the finite-size theorem.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that the Fibonacci duality defect in the critical golden chain carries an exact categorical fingerprint at finite lattice size, with fixed cut-charge weights and boundary entropy (log g = log φ) without finite-size extrapolation, proven via a finite-dimensional operator identity and Perron-Frobenius theorem.
AI.motivation: To show that non-invertible defects can be diagnosed exactly at finite lattice size (without scaling extrapolation) using categorical fingerprints, specifically for the Fibonacci duality defect in the critical golden chain.
AI.method: The proof uses a finite-dimensional operator identity for sandwiched cut projectors combined with a Perron-Frobenius sector theorem for the even-length ground state, establishing fixed cut-charge weights P_τ/P_1 = φ² and log g = log φ.
AI.result: The even-length antiferromagnetic ground state yields exact categorical data: P_τ/P_1 = φ² and log g = log φ, with no finite-size extrapolation needed. This two-charge result is separated from the finer six-primary tricritical-Ising resolution.
AI.conclusion: A sharp lattice-level boundary entropy for a non-Abelian duality defect is obtained, showing exact categorical fingerprints exist at finite lattice size for the Fibonacci defect.

title: Continuous Observation of Quantum Systems
comment: 35 pages. Appeared in "Communicating the Quantum Way, Contributions in Honor of Alexander S Holevo's 80th Birthday" (World Scientific 2026)
summary: In a series of papers in the 1980's Alexander Holevo proved a classification theorem for continuous quantum measurement processes, or, as they would today be called, stationary quantum trajectories in continuous time. His main tools were functional analytic in character: starting from a Bochner-type inequality he employed dilation techniques for positive definite kernels. Here we give an alternative, more probabilistic proof: we use weak convergence of measures and employ Levy's Continuity Theorem. We clarify the boundedness conditions in Holevo's theorem, and supply a simple example from quantum optics.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a new probabilistic proof of Holevo's classification theorem for continuous quantum measurement processes using weak convergence and Lévy's Continuity Theorem, replacing the original functional analytic approach. It clarifies boundedness conditions and provides a quantum optics example.
AI.motivation: To provide an alternative, more accessible probabilistic proof of Holevo's classification theorem for continuous quantum measurements, clarifying boundedness conditions that were implicit in the original functional analytic treatment.
AI.method: Uses weak convergence of measures and Lévy's Continuity Theorem as alternative mathematical tools to replace the original Bochner-type inequality and dilation techniques for positive definite kernels.
AI.result: An alternative probabilistic proof of Holevo's classification theorem for stationary quantum trajectories, with clarified boundedness conditions and a concrete example from quantum optics.
AI.conclusion: The probabilistic approach offers a more intuitive understanding of Holevo's classification results and clarifies the boundedness conditions that were less transparent in the original functional analytic framework.

title: Non-Clifford Benchmarking via Ensemble Feature Selection
summary: We propose an Ensemble Feature Selection (EFS) method for fast estimation of process infidelity of involutory multi-qubit gates, including non-Clifford targets, for which standard Clifford-based benchmarking does not apply. The method selects a compact set of experimentally executable circuit measurements from a candidate pool through offline training on a physically motivated ensemble of noisy channels, and combines them into a linear estimator with weights learned by ridge regression. The training ensemble is an explicit and tunable component of the protocol, incorporating prior knowledge about dominant hardware noise mechanisms. The estimator is validated on ibm_kingston using two Clifford validation benchmarks structurally related to the transpiled CCZ circuit, against independent Interleaved Randomized Benchmarking (IRB). Both show close EFS-IRB agreement across a wide range of process infidelities, with an estimation precision of approximately 0.01 over a process infidelity range of 0.02-0.2. EFS is subsequently applied directly to CCZ on the same device.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an Ensemble Feature Selection (EFS) method for fast estimation of process infidelity of involutory multi-qubit gates, including non-Clifford targets, using offline-trained linear estimators with ridge regression and validated on ibm_kingston against Interleaved Randomized Benchmarking.
AI.motivation: Standard Clifford-based benchmarking does not apply to non-Clifford target gates (e.g., CCZ), motivating the need for a fast and accurate infidelity estimation method that works for involutory multi-qubit gates beyond the Clifford set.
AI.method: EFS selects a compact set of experimentally executable circuit measurements from a candidate pool via offline training on a physically motivated ensemble of noisy channels, then combines them into a linear estimator with weights learned by ridge regression. The training ensemble incorporates prior knowledge about dominant hardware noise mechanisms.
AI.result: Validated on ibm_kingston using two Clifford validation benchmarks related to the transpiled CCZ circuit against independent IRB. EFS and IRB show close agreement across a process infidelity range of 0.02-0.2 with an estimation precision of approximately 0.01. EFS was then applied directly to CCZ on the same device.
AI.conclusion: EFS provides a fast and accurate method for estimating process infidelity of involutory multi-qubit gates, including non-Clifford targets, with precision comparable to IRB but applicable where IRB cannot be used.

title: Exploiting Symmetry in Quantum Reservoir Computing
summary: Symmetry is a powerful inductive bias, but in quantum reservoir computing (QRC) it cannot be imposed only by making the reservoir symmetric. QRC maps inputs through fixed quantum dynamics into nonlinear expectation-value features and trains only a classical readout, so the relevant symmetry must be visible in the measured feature map. We study cyclic forecasting tasks, such as sensors around a turbine or weather stations along a latitude circle, where the same local pattern should be forecast by the same rule wherever it appears on the ring. Thus, rotating the input by one site should rotate, not change, the predicted field. We show that a symmetric Hamiltonian is not enough: even large Pauli measurement sets can fail if their channels do not match the data symmetry, since optimization cannot recover channels that were never measured. We address this through observable-orbit completion, which measures symmetry-related observable channels and aligns encoding, dynamics, measurement, and readout. The strongest gains arise from aligning all four interfaces together, with matched spin-ring, real-weather, and IBM hardware checks supporting the same measured-span mechanism.

AI.tldr: Symmetry in quantum reservoir computing requires alignment across encoding, dynamics, measurement, and readout; simply symmetrizing the Hamiltonian is insufficient. We propose observable-orbit completion to match data symmetry, validated on cyclic forecasting tasks and IBM hardware.
AI.motivation: Symmetry is a powerful inductive bias for QRC, but it cannot be imposed solely by making the reservoir Hamiltonian symmetric—the symmetry must be visible in the measured feature map, which is the only part used by the classical readout.
AI.method: We study cyclic forecasting tasks and propose observable-orbit completion, which measures symmetry-related observable channels to align encoding, dynamics, measurement, and readout, ensuring the symmetry of the data is reflected in the feature map.
AI.result: Symmetric Hamiltonian alone is insufficient; large Pauli measurement sets can still fail if channels do not match data symmetry. The strongest gains come from aligning all four interfaces (encoding, dynamics, measurement, readout), validated on spin-ring, real-weather, and IBM hardware experiments.
AI.conclusion: Aligning encoding, dynamics, measurement, and readout via observable-orbit completion is essential for symmetry-aware QRC; the measured-span mechanism is key to achieving performance gains.

title: Non-signaling assistance in prepare-and-measure scenarios with classical communication
summary: Extracting the full power of non-local correlations in prepare-and-measure (PM) scenarios requires precise control over the timing and structure of the receiver's measurements. Indeed, recent developments in entanglement-assisted classical communication scenarios have shown that adaptive strategies-where the receiver uses the transmitted message to guide their measurement choice-can outperform standard non-adaptive protocols. Moving beyond quantum theory, however, the ultimate limits of such advantages remain largely unexplored. In this work, we thoroughly study adaptive and non-adaptive non-signaling (NS) assistance in PM scenarios with classical communication. We provide simple characterizations of the sets of behaviors that can be realized using both non-adaptive and adaptive NS assistance in arbitrary PM scenarios. As a consequence, we show that non-adaptive NS assistance is already strong enough to reproduce quantum communication with the same message dimension: the transmission of a qudit can be simulated by a classical dit assisted non-adaptively by NS correlations. We then compare adaptive and non-adaptive NS assistance. We prove that any adaptive NS advantage can be traced back to scenarios in which the receiver has no measurement choice, ruling out the genuinely multi-setting advantages found in entanglement-assisted quantum protocols. Finally, we identify all PM scenarios where adaptive NS strategies provide a strict advantage over non-adaptive ones.

AI.tldr: This paper studies adaptive vs. non-adaptive non-signaling (NS) assistance in prepare-and-measure (PM) scenarios with classical communication, showing that non-adaptive NS can simulate qudit transmission, proving adaptive advantages reduce to single-setting scenarios, and identifying when adaptive NS strictly outperforms non-adaptive.
AI.motivation: To explore the ultimate limits of adaptive vs. non-adaptive non-signaling assistance beyond quantum theory in prepare-and-measure scenarios.
AI.method: The authors provide simple characterizations of realizable behavior sets for both adaptive and non-adaptive NS assistance in arbitrary PM scenarios, and compare their power theoretically.
AI.result: Non-adaptive NS can simulate qudit transmission via classical dit; adaptive NS advantages reduce to scenarios with no measurement choice; they identify all PM scenarios where adaptive strictly outperforms non-adaptive.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive advantages in NS-assisted PM scenarios are not as rich as in entanglement-assisted quantum protocols; non-adaptive NS is already powerful enough to reproduce quantum communication.

title: Diverse efficiency of observable optimization for four-level quantum systems with higher-order traps
comment: This work is original preprint. Published version was significantly extended
summary: In this work, we perform an analytical and numerical analysis of quantum landscapes for controlling special four-level quantum systems for which we prove that the null control is a five-order trap: a $V-V$ system and an anharmonic system. As a control goal, an observable optimization is considered. The rigorous theoretical analysis is followed by the numerical experiments based on the GRadient Ascent Pulse Engineering (GRAPE) algorithm and Gradient Projection Method (GPM), performed to investigate the behavior of the efficiency of optimization for unconstrained (using GRAPE) and constrained (using GPM) controls. As the main result, we observe an interesting phenomenon with a diverse behavior of the optimization efficiency depending on the system Hamiltonian -- sharp increase of the optimization efficiency up to 100% at certain distance from the null control for a V-V system, while much slower and less significant increase (and even small decrease) for a system with the chain interaction. This sharp difference might be related with the fine structure of the subspace of controls where second derivative of the objective functional is zero.

AI.tldr: The paper analytically and numerically studies quantum control landscapes for two four-level systems (V-V and anharmonic), finding that null control is a five-order trap. Using GRAPE and GPM, they observe a sharp 100% optimization efficiency increase for the V-V system at certain distances from null control, contrasting with slower changes in chain-interaction systems, linked to zero second-derivative control subspaces.
AI.motivation: To understand the analytical and numerical properties of quantum control landscapes for special four-level quantum systems, specifically investigating the nature of the null control as a high-order trap and the optimization efficiency behavior under constrained and unconstrained controls.
AI.method: Analytical proof that null control is a five-order trap for V-V and anharmonic systems; numerical experiments using GRAPE (unconstrained) and GPM (constrained) to study optimization efficiency.
AI.result: A sharp increase in optimization efficiency up to 100% at a certain distance from null control for the V-V system, versus a much slower, less significant increase (and even a small decrease) for chain-interaction systems.
AI.conclusion: The sharp difference in optimization efficiency behavior may be related to the fine structure of the control subspace where the second derivative of the objective functional vanishes.

title: Polynomial equivalence of the global transverse-field Ising model and the gate model of quantum computation
summary: The transverse-field Ising model has attracted a lot of attention in recent years, especially in the quantum simulation and quantum computation literature. This interest is driven by many platforms for analog quantum computation, which implement the transverse-field Ising model for solving optimization problems, such as quantum annealing. However, it has remained an open question whether the Ising model with a global transverse field is equivalent to the gate model of quantum computation. Here we answer this question affirmatively for the case of a non-monotonic time-dependent transverse field. Building on a recent result by Cesa and Pichler on global control of Rydberg atoms, we provide a construction that allows simulating arbitrary quantum circuits using the Ising model with global transverse field with polynomial overhead in time, qubit number, and energy scale. Although the polynomial overheads we establish here are large relative to what is feasible on real-world quantum hardware, our result motivates the development of more sophisticated methods for simulating quantum circuits using the Ising model with a global transverse field. Additionally, under the assumption that quantum computing is strictly more powerful than classical computing, our result serves as a no-go theorem for efficient classical simulation of the transverse-field Ising model with a time-dependent global transverse field. Therefore, our finding is relevant for multiple communities, from analog quantum simulation and quantum optimization on various platforms to complexity and control theory.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the transverse-field Ising model with a non-monotonic time-dependent global field is computationally equivalent to the gate model of quantum computation, establishing polynomial overhead in time, qubit number, and energy scale for simulating arbitrary quantum circuits.
AI.motivation: The transverse-field Ising model is widely used in analog quantum computation and quantum annealing for optimization, but whether it is equivalent to the universal gate model of quantum computation remained an open question.
AI.method: Building on a recent result by Cesa and Pichler on global control of Rydberg atoms, the authors provide a constructive mapping that simulates arbitrary quantum circuits using the Ising model with a global transverse field, achieving polynomial overhead.
AI.result: The construction demonstrates that the transverse-field Ising model with non-monotonic time-dependent global field is universal for quantum computation, with polynomial overhead in time, qubit number, and energy scale.
AI.conclusion: This result serves as a no-go theorem for efficient classical simulation of the transverse-field Ising model (assuming quantum supremacy), motivates improved simulation methods, and bridges analog quantum simulation, quantum optimization, complexity theory, and control theory.
